lessons.title: Market Structure Explained: BOS vs CHOCH
lessons.summary: Mark swing highs and lows the way the episode does, read trend, range and transition from them, and name a break of structure or a change of character from a candle close rather than a feeling.
lessons.html:
Pound-dollar has been climbing all morning. Then one candle drops hard through a recent low. Depending on which trading video you watched last night, that move is a BOS, a CHOCH or an MSS. Three acronyms, one candle, and a comment section arguing about which is right.

This lesson does what the episode does: it ignores the acronyms until it has worked out what price actually did. Once you can read the structure, the labels mostly sort themselves out. Every later idea in Smart Money Concepts, from liquidity to fair value gaps to order blocks, is described relative to structure. A sweep of which high? A gap inside which leg? Get this part right and the rest has somewhere to stand.

We will use the same habit as every episode in the series. Two lines for every event. What the chart observably shows, which anyone can check. And what the Smart Money framework calls it, which is a label. Both are useful. They are not the same thing. Price first. Framework second.

Our teaching convention

Definitions vary between educators. Some count wicks, some count bodies, some only count the biggest swings. None of those choices is wrong. What is wrong is not making one. Here is the convention the episodes use, and the one this course uses everywhere:

  • Swing high: a candle whose high is higher than the highs of the two candles either side of it. A swing low is the mirror: a low lower than the two candles either side.
  • Confirmation: a swing exists only once the second candle after it has closed. Until then it is a candidate.
  • Swings are marked on wicks; breaks are judged on closes. Two different jobs, two different parts of the candle.
  • BOS (break of structure): a candle closes beyond the last swing in the direction of the trend.
  • CHOCH (change of character): the first close beyond the last swing against the trend. A warning, not a verdict.

Write those down before you open a chart. Everything below is just applying them.

Swing highs and swing lows

Start with a naked chart. No indicators, no boxes. Just candles. Now look for the turning points.

Why two candles each side? One candle each side marks almost every wobble; on an ordinary hourly chart you can end up with dozens of "swings" in a day. Five candles each side ignores almost everything and leaves you with two or three. Two is a middle setting. It is not magic. It is a choice, and the important thing is that it is written down, so that you mark the same chart the same way on Monday as on Friday.

Now the part a finished chart hides. Because of the two-candle rule, a swing is confirmed two candles late. Watch it in real time: here is a high. Is it a swing? Not yet. One lower candle. Still not. Two lower candles. Now it is. That delay is the honest version. Anything faster is borrowing candles from the future.

The same delay cuts the other way. A low can look perfect for one candle and then be undercut by the next. It was never a swing. On a finished chart you will not see that candidate at all, which is exactly why structure always looks easier in hindsight than it is live.

KEY POINT

A swing is a candidate until the second candle after it closes. Mark it then, not before.

Higher highs, lower lows and ranges

Connect the confirmed swings and you get the shape the chart has been drawing.

When each swing high is above the last one, and each swing low is above the last one, that is an uptrend: higher high, higher low, higher high, higher low. The higher lows matter as much as the highs. Each one is a place where price turned back up before reaching the previous low. Every pullback stopped short. That is what makes the trend a trend.

Flip it and you have a downtrend: lower low, lower high, lower low, lower high. Every rally stops short of the last high.

Notice how simple the question becomes. Is the sequence still intact? Yes or no. You do not need a forecast to answer it. You need the last two highs and the last two lows.

Then there is the market nobody puts in a thumbnail: no sequence at all. Highs and lows that go nowhere in particular. That is a range, and inside a range the little breaks mean very little. Price closes above a small high, then below a small low, and nothing has really changed. In a range, it is the edges that matter.

When a range ends, structure does not announce it in one candle. Price closes beyond an edge, holds there, and then starts printing swings in one direction. Only when two highs and two lows line up is there a sequence again. So at any moment structure is doing one of three things: trending, ranging, or changing from one to the other. Most of the acronyms you have heard are attempts to name that third state.

What is a BOS?

Break of structure, said "B-O-S". In our convention a BOS is a candle closing beyond the last swing in the direction of the existing trend. In an uptrend, a close above the last swing high. In a downtrend, a close below the last swing low.

Higher highs, higher lows. Price closes above the last swing high: BOS. And again. Each one is the trend confirming itself. In a downtrend you watch for the mirror: the trend makes a lower low, bounces to a lower high, then a candle closes below that lower low. The sequence just extended itself by one more step.

A close, not a wick

A wick that pokes above a high and falls back has not broken anything. It has visited. What those visits mean is the subject of the liquidity episodes; for now the rule is simply: wick equals visit, close equals break.

The same applies to a sudden spike. A news candle that rips through a high and closes back below it is still a wick. Big, fast, dramatic and, structurally, a visit.

Time does not break structure either. A trend that goes quiet for a day is still intact until a candle closes through the swing that matters.

And notice what a BOS is not. It is not an entry. By the time the close prints, the move that broke the high has already happened. A BOS tells you the trend is still working. It does not tell you where to get on.

Strong low, weak high

After a break of structure, the low that launched that break is the one the trend now depends on. Many SMC traders call it the strong low. The latest high, which has not produced a break yet, gets called the weak high.

Observably, the strong low is simply the swing the uptrend has to hold. Framework language just gives it a name. Same chart, same fact, one extra word.

KEY POINT

The important fact is never the acronym. It is which swing actually broke.

What is a CHOCH?

Change of character. Usually written CHOCH and usually said "chock". In our convention it is the first close beyond the last swing on the other side. In an uptrend, that is a close below the last higher low. In a downtrend, a close above the last lower high.

Look at how it usually builds. The trend makes a high. The next push fails to get above it: a lower high. Then price closes below the last higher low. That close is the change of character.

The lower high is often the first clue. But remember, it is only confirmed two candles after it prints. The close through the higher low is the event you can actually point to.

It is an early warning that the sequence has stopped working. A warning. Not a verdict. Try it before you read on.

Here is what happened next in that drill. Price turned round and closed above the old high anyway. The warning was wrong, and that is a perfectly normal outcome.

A change of character tells you the old sequence broke. It does not tell you a new one has started. That takes more structure: a lower high, a lower low, and time. When a trend genuinely ends, structure usually tells the story in three steps:

  1. A high that fails to go higher (a lower high, or a high that is only visited by a wick).
  2. A close through the last higher low: the CHOCH.
  3. A lower low, and then a lower high under it.

One step is a warning. Three is a new sequence.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating a CHOCH as a reversal signal. It is the end of the evidence for the old trend, not the start of evidence for a new one. Between the two there is often a stretch where the honest answer is "no sequence".

Going deeper

Why the delay is a feature. Many indicators and scripts that label structure on a finished chart quietly use the future: they mark a swing high at the candle where it happened, not at the candle where it became knowable. In replay or live, those labels appear two candles later than they seem to. If you backtest your structure rules, make the label appear on the confirming candle. Otherwise every result you get is a little bit better than reality.

Which swing is "the last swing on the other side"? In an uptrend it is the most recent confirmed higher low, the one that launched the latest break of structure. That is the same swing the framework calls the strong low. A smaller dip that never qualified as a two-candle swing does not count. Episode 2 shows why that one detail settles most arguments.

Close beyond by how much? Our convention says any close beyond. That is deliberate: it keeps the rule mechanical. Some traders add a buffer (a few pips, or a fraction of the average range) to avoid one-pip "breaks". If you add one, add it to both BOS and CHOCH, write the number down and never adjust it mid-trade.

Timeframe is part of the definition. A BOS on the 15-minute chart and a BOS on the 4-hour chart are different statements. Always record the timeframe with the label: "H1 BOS", "M15 CHOCH". Episode 2 shows the same eight hours being bullish and bearish at once, depending on which chart you look at.

What the framework says versus what you can see. The framework sometimes describes a CHOCH as the moment large players switched sides. What you can see is narrower and more useful: the market failed to hold the last low it had defended. You do not need a story about motives to respect that fact, and you should not trade the story when the fact is all you have.

THE RULES
  • Swings: a high (low) above (below) the two candles each side, confirmed only when the second candle after it has closed.
  • Swings are marked on wicks. Breaks are judged on closes. A wick beyond a swing is a visit, not a break.
  • BOS: a close beyond the last swing in the direction of the trend. It confirms the trend; it is not an entry.
  • CHOCH: the first close beyond the last swing against the trend. It is a warning, not a verdict.
  • In a range there is no sequence, so there is no BOS or CHOCH inside it. Only the edges count.
  • Write the convention down before you look at the chart, and record the timeframe with every label.

Summary

  • Structure is a sequence of confirmed swings: two candles each side, confirmed two candles later.
  • Higher highs and higher lows is an uptrend; lower lows and lower highs is a downtrend; no sequence is a range.
  • A BOS is a close beyond the last swing with the trend. It says the trend is still working; it is not an entry.
  • A CHOCH is the first close through the last swing against the trend. It says the old sequence broke, not that a new one has started.
  • Wick equals visit. Close equals break. Price first, framework second.

quiz.q: Under the episode's convention, when does a swing high become a confirmed swing?
options: As soon as the candle closes
When the next candle closes lower
When the second candle after it has closed without exceeding it
When price breaks the previous low
quiz.why: A swing needs two candles each side, so it can only be confirmed once the second candle after it has closed. Anything sooner borrows candles from the future.

quiz.q: In an uptrend, a news candle trades 30 pips above the last swing high and closes back below it. What is it structurally?
options: A BOS
A CHOCH
A visit: no break, because there was no close above
An MSS
quiz.why: Breaks are judged on closes. However dramatic the wick, a candle that closes back below the high has only visited it.

quiz.q: What does a BOS tell you?
options: Where to enter
That the trend is still working
That a reversal is due
That the strong low has been broken
quiz.why: A BOS confirms the existing trend. By the time it prints, the move has already happened, so on its own it gives no entry.

quiz.q: Price makes a lower high and then closes below the last higher low. Which statement is correct?
options: A downtrend has started
It is a CHOCH: the old sequence broke, but a new one has not started yet
It is a BOS
Nothing has happened until a wick goes lower
quiz.why: The close through the higher low is a change of character. A new downtrend still needs a lower low and a lower high under it.

quiz.q: Inside a sideways range, price closes above a small internal high. What is the best description?
options: A bullish BOS
A CHOCH
Mostly noise: in a range only the edges matter
A confirmed uptrend
quiz.why: A range has no sequence, so there is no structure to break inside it. The event worth naming is a close beyond a range edge followed by new swings in one direction.

lessons.title: MSS Explained: When a CHOCH Becomes a Real Shift
lessons.summary: Decide whether a change of character qualifies as a market structure shift using two checkable extras, separate internal from external structure, and run the five-question structure checklist on any chart.
lessons.html:
Episode 1 gave you the break of structure and the change of character. This lesson finishes the job. When does a CHOCH become a real market structure shift? Which swings are internal, which are external, and why does an ordinary 15-minute chart "break structure" ten times in a day?

The conventions from Lesson 1 still apply, unchanged: swings are two candles each side and confirmed two candles later; swings are marked on wicks; breaks are judged on closes. A BOS is a close beyond the last swing with the trend. A CHOCH is the first close beyond the last swing against it.

What is an MSS?

Market structure shift, said "M-S-S". Some educators use it to mean exactly the same thing as a change of character. Others reserve it for something more decisive. In our convention, an MSS is a change of character with two extras:

  1. A sweep just before it. In a bearish case, price traded above the last high and closed back below it.
  2. Displacement on the break. The candle that closes through the last higher low has a body at least twice the average body of the previous ten candles.

Take the first extra with the usual two lines. Observably: price traded above the prior high and closed back below it. In framework language: buy-side liquidity was swept. The observable line is a fact anyone can check on the chart. The framework line is a name for it, and it carries a story about resting orders that you cannot see on a spot forex chart, because there is no central order book. Keep the fact; hold the story lightly.

The second extra is there because it is measurable. "It looked strong" is an adjective. "Its body was 43 pips against a ten-candle average of 4" is a number you can write down, and anyone can look back ten candles and check it. Not a drift. A shove.

A sweep, then displacement through the last higher low. That is the combination this model calls an MSS.

So, back to the opening chart of Episode 1, the pound-dollar candle that three different videos would label three different ways. It was the first close below the higher low, so it is a change of character. It came straight after the high was swept, and it broke with displacement, so we would call it an MSS. And some educators would simply call it a bearish break of structure. None of them is lying. They are using different definitions, which is why you write yours down.

KEY POINT

Don't trade the acronym. Trade the structural event.

BOS vs CHOCH vs MSS

Side by side:

  • BOS: a close beyond the last swing with the trend. It says: the trend is still working.
  • CHOCH: the first close beyond the last swing against the trend. It says: the old sequence broke.
  • MSS: that same CHOCH, straight after a sweep, broken with displacement. It says: the break was decisive.

And none of the three says what happens next. An MSS is a better-documented warning than a plain CHOCH, not a promise. Here is the version that should make you careful: a CHOCH with neither extra, traded as if it were a reversal.

That trade is the standard way structure labels cost money. Every part of the CHOCH definition was met: lower high, then a close below the last higher low. But nothing about it was decisive. There was no visit above the prior high and no candle that stood out from the ten before it. Price drifted, stalled and then broke the high instead. Structure on its own does not give you an entry, a stop or a target; later episodes build those, and they all lean on this.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating the label as the trade. A CHOCH, even an MSS, tells you about the sequence. It does not tell you where to get in, where you are wrong or where price is going.

Internal vs external structure

Zoom out on an uptrend. The biggest swings, the ones that define the whole move, are external structure. The smaller swings inside them are internal structure. Same chart, two scales. In the episode, five-candle swings show two lows that matter; two-candle swings show four.

Internal breaks happen all the time inside a healthy trend. External breaks are rarer, and they matter more. A common way to use the distinction: external structure for direction, internal structure for timing. Episodes 9 and 10 come back to that when we put timeframes in order.

That is really all you need from this distinction. Anything beyond it is vocabulary for its own sake.

Messy real structure

Real charts are rarely that tidy. Take an ordinary 15-minute chart and label every close beyond a one-candle swing. In the episode that produced ten breaks of structure on one fairly ordinary day. If every candle is breaking structure, structure has stopped being particularly informative.

Now use bigger swings, three candles each side, and require a sequence before anything counts as a break. The breaks worth naming drop to none.

Neither setting is wrong. But you have to choose it before the chart moves, not after. And when a chart is this messy on your setting, the honest options are a higher timeframe, or no trade.

Multi-timeframe structure

One more source of arguments. Pound-dollar on the 4-hour chart: higher highs, higher lows. Bullish. Now take the last two 4-hour candles, eight hours of price, and look at them on the 5-minute chart. Same prices, same eight hours, 96 five-minute candles. Lower highs, lower lows. Bearish.

Both are true. The 5-minute downtrend is a pullback inside the 4-hour uptrend. So "the trend" means nothing until you say which timeframe.

A simple way to keep them apart:

  • The higher timeframe answers where the market is going overall.
  • The lower timeframe answers what it is doing right now.

Neither one answers both. Writing "H4 up, M5 down" is a complete and honest description. Writing "the trend is down" is half a sentence.

Five structure mistakes

  1. Labelling every tiny candle break a BOS. You have seen that chart. If the label appears every few candles it carries no information.
  2. Ignoring which swing broke. An internal low and the low that defines the trend are not the same event, even if both get the same label.
  3. Calling every pullback a change of character. A pullback is the trend breathing. The change of character is a close through the last higher low.
  4. Switching timeframe until the structure agrees with you. Change timeframe long enough and one of them will eventually say yes.
  5. Marking structure afterwards. On a finished chart every swing looks obvious. In real time, a swing does not exist until two candles after it.

Bonus mistake: seeing a break of structure in the middle of a range. If there was no sequence to begin with, there was no structure to break.

Your turn: interactive example

Euro-dollar, one-hour chart. Higher highs, higher lows. First question: is the trend up? Yes. The sequence is intact. Now price dips, bounces, then closes below a small low. Is that a change of character? Decide before you reveal.

On one-candle swings, yes. But on the two-candle swings we have been using, that low isn't a swing at all. The higher low that defines the trend is still standing underneath it. So on our structure, nothing has changed, and a few candles later price closes above the high. Break of structure. The trend confirmed itself again.

One last question. If this trend were going to change character on our swings, where would it have to happen? At the dashed line: a close below the last higher low. Until that close prints, the sequence is intact.

The question was never which acronym to use. It was which swing broke.

The structure checklist

Five questions, every time:

  1. What are the meaningful swings?
  2. What is the current sequence?
  3. Did a significant swing actually break, on a close?
  4. Was that with the structure, or against it?
  5. On which timeframe?

Answer those and the label is easy. Skip them and no label will save you.

To practise, cover the right side of any chart and move forward one candle at a time. Mark each swing only when it is confirmed, and write the sequence down before you reveal the next candle. Ten minutes a day of this does more for your structure reading than any number of finished charts.

Going deeper

Measuring displacement properly. Use bodies, not ranges: a candle with a long wick and a small body is not displacement, however big it looks. Average the bodies of the ten candles before the break, not including it. If the ten-candle window includes a news spike, the average is inflated and the test gets harder to pass; that is acceptable, because a break that cannot stand out from a news-heavy hour is not decisive anyway. Write down the ratio, not just "yes".

How close is "straight after"? The sweep should be the last swing event before the break: no fresh higher high, no new higher low in between. If price swept the high, then rallied and printed a new higher low, the sweep belongs to the old sequence and the later break is a CHOCH without the first extra.

Two-candle breaks. Sometimes the shove comes over two candles of similar size. Our convention tests the candle that closes through the level. You can choose to test combined bodies instead, but then apply it to every break you mark, and record that you did.

Internal structure and the CHOCH level. In Lesson 1 a CHOCH was the first close through the last swing on the other side. On our two-candle convention that swing is usually internal from a higher timeframe's point of view. That is fine: it is a warning on this timeframe. Whether it means anything bigger depends on the external structure, which is why the checklist asks "which timeframe?" last and never skips it.

What the framework adds, and what it does not. The framework says the sweep took buy-side liquidity and the displacement shows large participants committing. What you can verify is that price failed above the old high and then moved through the defended low unusually fast. That is genuinely useful context. It is not knowledge of anyone's intent, and it is not a forecast.

THE RULES
  • MSS = a CHOCH straight after a sweep (traded beyond the last high or low and closed back inside), broken with displacement.
  • Displacement = the breaking candle's body is at least 2× the average body of the previous 10 candles.
  • BOS says the trend is still working; CHOCH says the old sequence broke; MSS says the break was decisive. None of them predicts.
  • External structure for direction, internal structure for timing.
  • Choose swing size and timeframe before the chart moves. A chart that is messy on your setting is a higher timeframe or no trade.
  • Structure gives context, not an entry, a stop or a target.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Swings marked on the agreed setting (two candles each side) and only once confirmed
  • Current sequence written down: up, down or range, with the timeframe
  • The break was a close, not a wick
  • The broken swing identified: internal or external, last swing with or against the trend
  • If calling an MSS: sweep immediately before, and breaking body at least 2× the ten-candle average
  • Higher-timeframe structure noted before acting on lower-timeframe structure

Summary

  • An MSS is a CHOCH with two checkable extras: a sweep just before it and a displaced breaking candle (body ≥ 2× the ten-candle average).
  • BOS, CHOCH and MSS describe what happened to the sequence. None of them predicts what happens next, and none is an entry.
  • External swings give direction; internal swings give timing. Internal breaks inside a healthy trend are normal.
  • Pick swing size and timeframe before the chart moves; on a messy chart the honest options are a higher timeframe or no trade.
  • Five questions: swings, sequence, break on a close, with or against, which timeframe.

quiz.q: Under the episode's convention, which two extras turn a CHOCH into an MSS?
options: A higher high and a retest
A sweep just before it and a breaking body at least 2× the 10-candle average
A fair value gap and an order block
Two closes beyond the level and rising volume
quiz.why: Our MSS is a CHOCH straight after a sweep of the last high (or low), broken with displacement measured as a body at least twice the average of the previous ten.

quiz.q: The ten candles before a break have an average body of 8 pips. The breaking candle has a 14-pip body and closes through the last higher low just after a sweep. What is it?
options: An MSS
A CHOCH, but not an MSS: 14 is less than 2 × 8
A BOS
Nothing, because it was not displaced
quiz.why: It is still a change of character (the first close through the last higher low). It fails the displacement test, which needs at least 16 pips, so it does not qualify as an MSS.

quiz.q: Inside a clear uptrend, price closes below a small internal low but stays well above the external low. What has changed for direction?
options: The trend is now down
An MSS has formed
Nothing for direction: internal breaks are normal; the external low still holds
The external low must now be moved
quiz.why: External structure gives direction. Internal breaks happen all the time in healthy trends and are useful for timing, not for flipping bias.

quiz.q: The H4 chart shows higher highs and higher lows. The last eight hours on M5 show lower highs and lower lows. Which description is correct?
options: The trend is down
The trend is up and the M5 is wrong
Both are true: an M5 downtrend that is a pullback inside the H4 uptrend
Neither: the timeframes cancel out
quiz.why: Different scale, different structure. 'The trend' means nothing until you name the timeframe.

quiz.q: In the drill, price closed below a low that had only one candle either side. On the course's two-candle convention, what was it?
options: A CHOCH
An MSS
Not a break of any swing: the small low was never a confirmed swing, and the real higher low was intact
A bearish BOS
quiz.why: A two-candle swing needs two candles either side. The small low did not qualify, so closing below it broke nothing on our structure. A CHOCH needed a close below the real higher low.

lessons.title: Stop Hunts Explained — What the Chart Actually Proves
lessons.summary: Define liquidity the way SMC uses it, mark buy-side and sell-side liquidity, and tell a sweep from a break on the close, the next candle and the retest.
lessons.html:
You are short Pound-dollar. Your stop sits just above two equal highs, exactly where the textbook told you to put it. Price spikes up, through the highs, through your stop. Then it falls, all the way to where your target was.

You were right about the direction. Price simply took your stop first. If that has happened more than once, it starts to feel personal: the same pattern, the stop just beyond the obvious line, a spike, out, and then the move you were waiting for.

Bad luck, or liquidity? This lesson follows episode 3 of the series. It separates what the chart actually shows from what Smart Money Concepts calls it, and it gives you two definitions you can apply to any candle: a sweep and a break. Price first. Framework second.

Why your stop gets hit first

Here is the opening chart from the film, rebuilt as a training chart. Look at where the stop was, not just at the spike.

Notice what the chart proves and what it does not. It proves that one candle traded above the equal highs and closed back below them. It proves the stop sat just beyond the most obvious line on the chart. It does not prove that anybody aimed at that stop. Keep those two lists apart for the rest of the lesson.

What liquidity actually means

The word is used two ways, and confusing them causes most of the nonsense you will read about it.

In normal market language, liquidity is how easily something can be bought or sold without moving the price much. Euro-dollar is very liquid. That is a fact about the market as a whole.

In Smart Money Concepts, liquidity usually means something narrower: clusters of orders likely to be resting at obvious places on the chart. Stop losses. Breakout entries. Pending orders.

Here is the honest part. On a spot forex chart you cannot see those orders. There is no central order book showing them. When an SMC chart draws a cluster of orders above a high, the cluster is illustrative: a reasonable assumption about where orders tend to sit, not a measurement.

Why would orders cluster at all? Because traders learn from the same textbooks. Put your stop beyond the last swing. Buy the breakout of the high. Sell the break of the low. When a great many people follow the same advice, their orders end up in the same few places.

What we can see is how price behaves when it reaches those places. That is the whole subject of this lesson and the next.

KEY POINT

In SMC, "liquidity" means likely order clusters at obvious levels. In spot FX they are assumed, never measured. What you can measure is the reaction.

Where liquidity sits

Start with the obvious places. Above swing highs. Below swing lows. These are the same swings from episode 1: a swing high is a candle whose high is above the two candles on each side, and it is only confirmed two candles later.

Then the places that look like walls:

  • Equal highs and equal lows. Two or more swings at almost the same price. In this series they count as equal if they are within one pip.
  • The previous day's high and low.
  • The edges of a range.
  • Session highs and lows — Asia, London, New York.
  • Older levels. Yesterday's high, last week's low. A level does not stop being obvious because it is a few days old.

If you can see a level easily, assume plenty of other people can too. Obvious level, crowded level. That is really the whole idea. Lesson 4 maps each of these in detail.

Buy-side vs sell-side (BSL / SSL)

Two labels you will see everywhere.

Buy-side liquidity (BSL) sits above highs. The orders resting there are mostly buy orders: stop losses on short trades are buy orders, and so are breakout entries from traders waiting to buy a new high.

Sell-side liquidity (SSL) sits below lows. It is the mirror: long traders' stops and breakdown entries are sell orders.

Put both on one chart and you will usually find price sitting between two pools. Part of the SMC approach is asking which one price is closer to, and which one it reached last.

Now the translation that keeps you honest. Observably, price is approaching a swing high. In framework language, it is approaching buy-side liquidity. Same event, two descriptions. When you write your trading notes, write the first one first.

Sweep vs breakout

This is the most useful distinction in the episode. Price trades through a high. Two very different things can happen next.

In our convention:

  • A sweep is a candle that trades beyond the level and closes back inside on the same candle. The level was taken, then rejected.
  • A break is a close beyond the level, followed by another close beyond. The level was taken and accepted.

Notice what the rule does not care about: how far beyond the level the wick went. One pip or fifteen, it is the close that decides which story you are looking at.

So what do you actually watch? Three things, in order:

  1. The close. Where did the candle that crossed the level close?
  2. The next candle. Did it close beyond as well, or back inside?
  3. The retest. If price came back to the level, which side did it hold from?
KEY POINT

Same level, same first move, opposite meaning. Taken is not broken.

And one warning. A close back inside is not the end of the story. A sweep can turn into a break two candles later: price closes back below the high, then closes above it twice, and keeps going. That is why a sweep on its own is information, not an instruction. The drill at the end of this lesson is exactly that case.

COMMON MISTAKE

Selling the close of the sweep candle. At that moment you do not know whether it is a sweep that will hold or the first leg of a break. That is the next candle's job.

Sweep vs grab

You will also hear "liquidity grab". Some educators use sweep and grab for the same thing. Others use grab for a fast spike through one level, and sweep for a move that clears several levels or a whole cluster.

There is no official dictionary. Terminology varies; what price did is what matters. In this series we use one word, sweep, with the definition above, and if someone else's video calls the same candle a grab, translate it and move on.

Stop hunts: what the chart can prove

Then there is the phrase that gets the most comments: the stop hunt.

Observably, price traded through an obvious level where stops were likely, and then reversed. That is all the chart shows.

Whether anyone set out to hit those stops on purpose, the chart cannot tell you. A level full of stop orders can be triggered by ordinary buying, by news, or by a single large order passing through. The candle looks the same either way. If every wick is manipulation, the market apparently has a personal vendetta against everyone.

The useful lesson is not who did it. It is where your stop was: just beyond the most obvious line on the chart. Traders deal with that in a few common ways:

  • Structure plus a buffer. Place the stop beyond the structure that would prove the idea wrong, plus a buffer, rather than a hair beyond the obvious line.
  • Smaller size, same risk. A wider stop with a smaller position costs the same in money. If you risk 1% of the account, a 30-pip stop simply means a smaller position than a 15-pip stop.
  • Wait for the sweep. Let the obvious level be taken before you enter at all.

None of these removes risk. They just stop you being the most predictable order on the chart.

Going deeper

Why the close, and why one candle. A rule that lets you decide after the fact is not a rule. "A sweep is any move through a level that later comes back" can relabel every failed breakout, at any distance, after you already know the answer. Tying the sweep to the close of the same candle, and the break to two consecutive closes, means you know which story you are in at a fixed, known moment. It also means the same chart can carry both labels in sequence: sweep at candle one, break at candle three. That is not a contradiction; it is the definition doing its job.

Timeframe matters. A sweep is judged on the timeframe where the level was marked. An H1 sweep candle can contain a fifteen-minute break and a fifteen-minute rejection inside it. If you mark the level on H1, judge it on H1 closes.

Depth is information, not a filter. The rule ignores wick depth on purpose, but you should still record it. If the sweeps on your pair and timeframe routinely reach eight or ten pips beyond the level, a stop three pips beyond that level is inside the zone price commonly visits. That is the arithmetic behind "structure plus a buffer".

The crowding twist. As SMC has become popular, its own favourite levels have become obvious too. The edge of a well-known zone collects stops of its own. Expect the same behaviour there that you see at equal highs.

What a sweep is not. It is not a reversal signal. Lesson 4 shows a sweep that did not reverse at all, and the one extra piece of evidence — a change of character — that separates the two.

THE RULES
  • Liquidity (SMC) = likely order clusters at obvious levels. In spot FX they are illustrative, never measured.
  • BSL sits above highs (buy orders); SSL sits below lows (sell orders).
  • Sweep = trades beyond the level and closes back inside on the same candle.
  • Break = a close beyond the level, then another close beyond.
  • Wick depth does not decide; the close does. A sweep can still become a break later.
  • A sweep is information, not an instruction. Never enter on the sweep candle alone.
  • Stops go beyond the structure that proves you wrong, plus a buffer; size the position to the stop.

Practice drill

Euro-dollar, one-hour chart. Price has traded above two equal highs and closed back below them. A short on the close looks tempting.

Summary

  • Market liquidity is ease of trading; SMC liquidity is likely order clusters at obvious levels — illustrative in spot FX, never measured.
  • Buy-side liquidity sits above highs; sell-side liquidity sits below lows. Obvious level, crowded level.
  • Sweep: through and close back inside on the same candle. Break: close beyond, then another close beyond. Watch the close, the next candle and the retest.
  • "Stop hunt" describes a chart event, not a proven intent. The fix is your own stop placement, not a villain.
  • Don't trade the wick. Trade the response.

quiz.q: In SMC language, what does 'liquidity' usually mean?
options: How fast a broker fills your order
Likely clusters of orders resting at obvious levels
The total daily volume of a currency pair
Any large candle
quiz.why: SMC narrows the word to likely order clusters at obvious places. Ease of trading is the normal market meaning; the other two are not liquidity at all.

quiz.q: Why is buy-side liquidity drawn above highs?
options: Because banks buy at highs
Because price always returns to highs
Because short traders' stops and breakout buy entries rest there, and both are buy orders
Because highs are where the spread widens
quiz.why: A stop on a short is a buy order, and so is a buy-stop breakout entry. Those orders are assumed to cluster above obvious highs.

quiz.q: A candle trades 15 pips above a swing high and closes 3 pips below it. In the series convention, what is it?
options: A break, because it went 15 pips through
A sweep, because it closed back inside on the same candle
Nothing until the third candle
A change of character
quiz.why: Depth does not decide. Trading beyond and closing back inside on the same candle is a sweep.

quiz.q: Price sweeps a high, then the next two candles both close above it. What should your notes now say?
options: Still a sweep: the first close decides forever
Stop hunt confirmed
The level is now broken: close beyond, then another close beyond
Invalid chart
quiz.why: A sweep can become a break. Two consecutive closes beyond the level meet the break rule, so the story has changed.

quiz.q: Your short was stopped two pips above equal highs before price fell to your target. Which conclusion does the chart actually support?
options: Your broker hunted your stop
Smart money targeted your order
Your stop sat just beyond the most obvious line on the chart, where many stops were likely to be
Equal highs never hold
quiz.why: The chart cannot show intent. It does show where your stop was, and that is the part you can change.

lessons.title: Where Liquidity Sits — Equal Highs, Sessions & Inducement
lessons.summary: Map equal highs and lows, the previous day's levels and the Asia, London and New York extremes, and combine a sweep with a change of character before treating it as a setup.
lessons.html:
Lesson 3 defined liquidity and gave you two words for what happens when price reaches it: a sweep (through, and a close back inside on the same candle) or a break (a close beyond, then another close beyond). This lesson follows episode 4. It shows where liquidity actually sits on a working chart, and what has to happen after price takes it before it is worth planning a trade.

The levels are not exotic. Equal highs and lows. A single candle at a level that matters. A small swing in front of a bigger one. Yesterday's high and low. The Asia range. What makes them useful is not that they are secret, but that they are obvious, and that you have written down in advance how you will judge the reaction.

Price first. Framework second.

Equal highs and equal lows

In this series, two swing highs count as equal if they are within one pip of each other. The same for lows. Swings use the series convention: a high above the two candles on each side, confirmed two candles later.

Observably, equal highs mean price has turned down from the same price twice. Many traders read that as resistance and place their stops just above it. So equal highs cut both ways: they look like a ceiling, and they are also exactly where a lot of buy orders are likely to be waiting. In framework language, buy-side liquidity.

The more often a level is tested, the more obvious it becomes. Three equal highs are more noticeable than two. That does not make them stronger. It makes them more crowded. Which one it turns out to be — a sweep or a break — you only find out from the reaction.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating a third touch as proof that a level is "strong". A third touch is proof that it is famous. Famous levels are where stops gather.

Banker candles and IFC

Now a term you will meet in SMC communities: the banker candle. You will also hear institutional funding candle (IFC) and single candle order block (SCOB). These are community terms, not standard market terminology, and different groups use the names in different ways.

For our teaching purposes, we mean one thing: a single candle that trades beyond a meaningful high or low, takes that level, and closes back inside. It leaves a visible rejection at a level that matters. In other words, it is a sweep candle — and it is only interesting because of where it is.

Compare the two. A pin bar in the middle of nowhere: no level, nothing taken. And the same shape sitting on a swing low it has just swept. And if a big candle at a level closes beyond it instead of back inside, it is not a sweep candle at all. It is a break. Same size, opposite story.

You will sometimes hear that these candles carry institutional volume. On spot forex there is no consolidated volume figure to check that against. What you can check is the level, the wick and the close. Shape alone is not the idea. Location is.

Inducement

Inducement is another framework term. The idea is that a small, obvious swing forms in front of a bigger level. Traders place orders around the small one. Price trades through it first, then heads towards the bigger level.

Observably: price took out a minor swing, then continued towards a major one. That is what you can see. The framework sometimes describes the minor swing as bait. Whether anyone placed it there deliberately is not something a chart can show.

What you can use is the order of events: small level first, big level second. Suppose a pullback in an uptrend has a minor swing low at 40 pips and the major swing low that defines the leg sits at 10 pips. Price trades below 40 and keeps going. In inducement language, the minor low was the inducement and the major low is still the level that matters. In plain language, the first sweep was not the important one, so you do not act on it. You keep watching the major low.

Internal vs external liquidity

This is the same idea as internal and external structure from episode 2. External liquidity sits beyond the big swings that define the dealing range: above the range high, below the range low. Internal liquidity sits inside the range: smaller swings, gaps and minor equal highs.

A common SMC description is that price moves between the two — from internal to external and back again. Treat that as a way of mapping the chart, not a law the market has to obey. It is useful because it tells you which levels are "inside" and therefore minor, and which are the edges a bigger move would need to reach.

Previous day high and low

One of the most widely watched pairs of levels in forex is yesterday's high and yesterday's low: PDH and PDL.

On one day, price pushes above PDH during the London morning, closes back below it, and spends the rest of the session lower. On another day, it closes above PDH, holds above it, and never looks back. Same level. Same first touch. Different day.

So the previous day's high is not a sell signal, and it is not a buy signal. It is a place to watch the reaction, using exactly the sweep and break rules from lesson 3.

Session liquidity: Asia, London, New York

For forex, sessions supply some of the most watched levels of the day. For this series, the Asia range runs from 00:00 to 06:59 London time. That is our choice, written down, so that your Asia high and low are the same every day and nobody can move them afterwards.

Here is one London morning. Price trades below the Asia low; in framework language, the sell-side liquidity is taken. The same candle closes back inside the range. Then the structure shifts: a close above the last lower high. In the film this is shown on the five-minute chart; the logic is identical on any timeframe, so long as you judge the shift on the timeframe you chose in advance. Now there is a sweep and a shift, and that is the start of a possible long. Not the trade itself. The start.

To be clear, this is not a rule that London sweeps Asia. Some days it does. Many days it does not. Some days it sweeps the high and the low. It also works the other way round: London trades above the Asia high, closes back inside, and the structure shifts down — buy-side taken, then a close below the last higher low.

The same thinking carries through the day. The London high and low become levels the New York session can trade through or respect. Each session's extremes are simply the next set of obvious lines.

Sweep + structure

This is the most important idea in the episode. A sweep on its own is not a reversal signal.

Here price took the level, bounced for two candles, and then kept falling. Compare it with the session chart above, where the sweep was followed by a close above the last lower high. In the second case the structure agrees with the sweep. In the first, it never did.

KEY POINT

The sweep tells you where something happened. The structure tells you whether it mattered.

Many SMC traders also talk about the draw on liquidity: the next obvious pool price might be heading for. If sell-side has just been taken below, the buy-side above becomes the possible draw. Episode 11 makes that a formal step. For now, notice that it is a possibility you plan around, not a destination price owes you.

Your turn: interactive example

Euro-dollar, one-hour chart. A downtrend into equal lows. Price trades below them and closes back above.

Pause and decide before you reveal. Then answer the second question too: if this does turn into a long, where is the next obvious pool of liquidity above?

Four liquidity mistakes

  1. Calling every wick a liquidity grab. If the wick is not at a level anyone was watching, it is just a wick.
  2. Entering on the sweep candle itself. At that moment you do not know whether it is a sweep or the start of a break. That is the next candle's job.
  3. Treating the opposite pool as a guaranteed target. Liquidity above does not oblige price to go and get it.
  4. Putting your own stop a hair beyond the most obvious line, and then being surprised. Lesson 3 started there. Do not finish there.

The liquidity checklist

Five checks, every time, in this order:

PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Location: is this an obvious level (equal highs/lows, PDH/PDL, session high/low, range edge, swing)?
  • Sweep: did price trade through it and close back inside on the same candle?
  • Reaction: what did the next candles do — stay inside, or close beyond twice (a break)?
  • Structure: did a meaningful swing break on a close (CHOCH against the prior move)?
  • Trigger: only now plan an entry; my own stop is beyond the structure plus a buffer, not a hair beyond the line

And for your own stops, the lesson works in reverse. If your stop sits just beyond the most obvious line on the chart, it is sitting where a lot of other stops are likely to be too.

Going deeper

Write the levels down before the session. Equal highs, PDH and PDL, and the Asia high and low are all knowable before London opens. Marking them in advance is analysis; "discovering" a level while price races towards it is usually adrenaline doing the drawing. Use the fixed Asia window (00:00–06:59 London) so your levels cannot drift.

Equal means one pip — on purpose. A tight, fixed tolerance stops you calling any two nearby highs "equal" after the fact. On a fast pair or a higher timeframe you will see fewer equal highs under this rule. That is fine: fewer, cleaner levels are the point.

Sweep, shift, and the order of evidence. The checklist order matters. A shift without a prior sweep at a meaningful level is just structure; a sweep without a shift is just a wick at a level. Episode 2's MSS is the strict version: a CHOCH that comes straight after a sweep and breaks with displacement — a body at least twice the size of the last ten. If you want a higher bar for a reversal, require the MSS, not just the CHOCH.

Inducement and the "which sweep?" problem. When there are several stacked lows, more than one will be swept on the way down. Decide in advance which one is the level that matters — normally the swing that defines the leg, or external liquidity — and treat sweeps of minor levels in front of it as information only.

The honest limits. None of this measures orders. Spot FX has no central order book, and no consolidated volume. Every statement in this lesson about clusters is an assumption about where orders tend to sit; every rule is about candles you can see. Keep it that way, and the framework stays testable.

THE RULES
  • Equal highs/lows: swing points within one pip of each other.
  • Asia range: 00:00–06:59 London time. Session extremes are levels, not signals.
  • A banker candle / IFC, in this course, is a sweep candle at a meaningful level — location, wick and close.
  • A sweep is not a reversal. Sweep + change of character is the start of a setup, not the trade.
  • The draw on liquidity is a possibility to plan around, never a promised destination.

Summary

  • Equal highs and lows (within one pip) are more obvious with each test — more crowded, not stronger.
  • A banker candle or IFC, as used here, is a sweep candle at a level that matters; shape alone is not the idea.
  • Inducement, internal/external liquidity, PDH/PDL and session extremes are all ways of listing obvious levels in advance.
  • Sweep tells you where; structure tells you whether. Wait for the change of character.
  • Run the five checks — location, sweep, reaction, structure, trigger — every time.

quiz.q: Two swing highs are 0.6 pips apart. Under the series rule, are they equal highs?
options: No — they must be identical
Yes — they are within one pip
Only if a third touch forms
Only on the daily chart
quiz.why: The series counts swing highs within one pip of each other as equal.

quiz.q: A level has been tested three times without breaking. What has the third test changed?
options: The level is now proven strong
The level is now more obvious and more crowded with stops
Price can no longer break it
Nothing at all
quiz.why: More tests make a level more noticeable, so more stops gather beyond it. It does not make it stronger.

quiz.q: What makes a candle a 'banker candle' in this course's teaching definition?
options: A body more than twice the average
Heavy institutional volume
It trades beyond a meaningful high or low and closes back inside
It forms at the London open
quiz.why: The course defines it by location, wick and close. Spot FX has no consolidated volume, and size or timing alone are not the idea.

quiz.q: In the drill, why was the right answer 'wait' when the sweep candle closed?
options: The equal lows were not equal
The last lower high was still standing — no change of character yet
It was the Asia session
The wick was too short
quiz.why: The sweep showed where; the structure had not yet said whether. Only the later close above the lower high made it a setup worth planning.

quiz.q: London trades below the Asia low and closes back inside. What is the correct next step?
options: Buy immediately — London always sweeps Asia
Sell — the low has broken
Watch for a close above the last lower high before treating it as a possible long
Ignore it — session levels do not matter
quiz.why: That is a sweep of session liquidity. It becomes the start of a possible long only if structure shifts. London sweeping Asia is not a rule.

lessons.title: Fair Value Gaps — The 4 Fs
lessons.summary: Find a bullish fair value gap with the three-candle wick rule, filter it with three fixed checks, wait for the fill, and fire only on a close back above the gap — with the stop, target and size decided before you enter.
lessons.html:
Price explodes upward and leaves a gap. You have heard the rule: price always comes back to fill the gap. So you put a buy order at the top of the gap and wait. Price comes back, fills your order, and keeps going. Your stop goes, and by the time the move finishes price is 31 pips below where you bought.

Nothing about that trade was unusual. Gaps get filled all the time. Sometimes price bounces out of them and sometimes it slices straight through, and the gap on its own cannot tell you which. What price does when it gets back there can. This lesson turns that sentence into four rules you can follow on any chart: Find, Filter, Fill, Fire.

What a fair value gap is

Start with what you can see. Take any three consecutive candles. In a bullish fair value gap, the low of candle 3 is above the high of candle 1. The prices between those two wicks were traded only by candle 2, on its way up. The gap is that band: from candle 1's high to candle 3's low.

Two details matter more than they look.

Use the wicks, not the bodies. The definition compares candle 1's high with candle 3's low. Bodies leave you with a judgement call about where the "real" gap is; wicks do not. Two traders looking at the same chart should mark exactly the same band, to the pip.

Candle 2 is the move. A gap only exists because the middle candle travelled far enough that its neighbours could not overlap. So the size of candle 2 is part of the story, and the filter below measures it.

Now the framework layer. In SMC language the gap is called an imbalance: the idea is that the move was so one-sided that the market "left business undone" and will be "drawn back" to it. You will also hear the gap described as the footprint a displacement move leaves behind. That last phrase is useful, as long as you keep it at the level of description: a fast, one-sided move happened here. It is not evidence of who was buying, and no rule of the market obliges price to return.

Price first. Framework second. What the chart shows is a fast move and a band of price that was crossed once. Everything else is interpretation, and the 4 Fs are built so that you never need the interpretation to make a decision.

KEY POINT

A bullish fair value gap is the band between candle 1's high and candle 3's low, when candle 3's low is above candle 1's high. Wicks, not bodies.

The framework: the 4 Fs

The whole method fits on one line:

  1. Find — three candles; candle 3's low is above candle 1's high. Use the wicks.
  2. Filter — keep the gap only if all three checks hold: the middle candle's body is at least 2 × the average body of the previous 10 candles; the move closes above the highest high of the previous 12 candles; the gap is at least 3 pips.
  3. Fill — wait for price to come back into the gap within 20 candles. Don't chase.
  4. Fire — buy only when a candle dips into the gap and closes back above its top. Stop 2 pips under the gap. Target 2R. A close below the gap first means the gap has failed.

The fair value gap has no single official definition, and educators disagree about the details. These numbers are one fixed, testable version chosen for teaching. Their value is not that they are magic; it is that they are written down, so you cannot quietly change them after you see what price did.

Keep one sentence from this lesson if you keep nothing else: the gap is where you look; the reaction is why you act.

F1 — Find

Finding is mechanical. Walk the chart three candles at a time and ask one question: is candle 3's low above candle 1's high? If yes, mark the band between them. If the wicks touch or overlap, there is no gap, however big candle 2 looks.

You will find a lot of them. On a busy intraday chart, small gaps appear every few hours, many inside ranges where nothing of interest is happening. That is fine. Finding is meant to be generous. The next step is meant to be strict.

F2 — Filter

The filter asks whether the gap was left by a move that mattered. Each check has a plain-English reason behind it.

  • Body at least 2× the average of the previous 10. This is the displacement test. A gap left by a candle that is only slightly bigger than its neighbours is a normal candle in a normal market. Measure the middle candle's body (open to close, not the wicks) against the average body of the 10 candles before it.
  • Close above the highest high of the previous 12 candles. The move has to break something. A gap that forms in the middle of a range, below the recent highs, records a fast candle and nothing more.
  • Gap at least 3 pips. Below that, spread and ordinary noise swallow the band, and a stop "2 pips under the gap" sits almost on top of your entry.

All three must hold. Two out of three is a fail. In the episode, one chart carries nine gaps and only two of them survive. That ratio is normal, and it is the point of the step.

COMMON MISTAKE

Grading the gap by how it looks. A gap that "feels strong" but fails one check is a fail. The filter exists precisely so that your mood does not get a vote.

F3 — Fill

A filtered gap is a candidate, not a trade. Step three is waiting for price to come back into it — and allowing it 20 candles to do so. If price has not traded back into the band within 20 candles of the gap forming, the gap is retired and you move on.

The rule cuts both ways. It stops you buying the breakout in a hurry because you are afraid of missing the move: you do not chase. And it stops you sitting on a stale gap for days, waiting for a return that has long since stopped meaning anything about the move that made it.

Some valid gaps never come back. That is not a failure of the method. A filtered gap that runs away without you costs nothing, and over time you will see plenty of them.

F4 — Fire, plus stop, target and size

The fill is not the signal. The reaction is. You buy only when a candle dips into the gap and closes back above its top. That close is the observable evidence that price visited the band and was pushed back out of it. A blind order resting at the gap, like the one at the start of this lesson, buys whatever happens next — including a slice straight through.

The other half of the rule is just as important: if a candle closes below the gap before any candle closes back above it, the gap has failed. Cancel it. Do not wait for "a better reaction" lower down.

Once the trigger candle closes, the trade writes itself:

  • Entry: the close of the reaction candle.
  • Stop: 2 pips under the bottom of the gap (candle 1's high).
  • Target: 2R — twice the distance from entry to stop.
  • Size: fixed risk. Decide the money you are prepared to lose, divide by the stop in pips.

Here are the numbers from the worked example used in this series. The gap runs from 1.08626 to 1.08708. The reaction candle dips in and closes at 1.08738. The stop goes 2 pips under the gap, at 1.08606: a 13.2-pip stop. The target is 2R, 26.4 pips above entry.

On an illustrative £2,000 account risking 1%, the risk is £20. £20 ÷ 13.2 pips ≈ £1.52 a pip. If the stop is hit you lose about £20; if the target is hit you make about £40, before costs. The size changes from trade to trade because the stop does. The risk does not.

Why 2R? Because of the break-even arithmetic. With a 2R target and a 1R loss, one win pays for two losses, so roughly a third of trades need to reach the target just to break even before costs. That is not a promise that a third will; it is the bar the method has to clear on your own testing, and it tells you how much losing to expect along the way.

Up next

The 4 Fs give you a decision you can repeat. They do not give you certainty. The next episode puts them under pressure: the trap from the start of this lesson re-run through the rules, a trade that passes all four Fs and still loses, and one full trade from the first candle to the target.

Going deeper

Why fixed numbers. Every threshold in the filter — 2×, 10 candles, 12 candles, 3 pips, 20 candles, 2 pips, 2R — could reasonably be something else. What cannot change is the order of events: write the numbers down, then test, then judge. Adjusting a threshold after a loss so that the loss "would have been filtered out" is curve-fitting by hand, and it guarantees your notes describe a method you never actually traded.

Partial versus full fill. The rules ask for price to enter the gap, not to fill it. Strong moves often dip into the top of a gap and leave; a limit order at the bottom of the gap would miss them. That is one reason F4 uses a close back above the top as the trigger rather than a resting order at a chosen depth: you do not have to guess how far price will go into the band. The price of that choice is a slightly worse entry than the best possible fill.

The bearish mirror. Everything here is written for buys. The mirror image is a bearish gap — candle 1's low above candle 3's high — with the break check flipped to a close below the lowest low of the previous 12 candles, the fire rule flipped to a close back below the gap's bottom, and the stop 2 pips above the gap. If you trade both directions, test both directions separately.

Failed gaps. When a candle closes through the far side of the gap first, the gap has failed. Some traders then treat the failed band as resistance on a retest from below, an idea sometimes called an inversion gap. It is outside these rules; treat it as a separate idea you would have to define and test on its own.

Context still matters. The filter checks that the move was large and broke something. It does not check what the higher timeframe is doing or which liquidity the move took. Later episodes add those layers. For now, the 4 Fs stand alone, so that you can test them alone.

THE RULES
  • Find: candle 3's low above candle 1's high. Wicks, not bodies.
  • Filter: middle body at least 2× the average of the previous 10; the move closes above the highest high of the previous 12 candles; gap at least 3 pips. All three, or no.
  • Fill: price must come back into the gap within 20 candles. Don't chase.
  • Fire: buy only on a close back above the gap after a dip into it. A close below the gap first means the gap has failed.
  • Stop 2 pips under the gap. Target 2R. Size from a fixed risk per trade.

Summary

  • "Price always fills the gap" is not a rule you can trade: gaps get filled, and then price can bounce or slice through.
  • A bullish fair value gap is the band between candle 1's high and candle 3's low. Wicks, not bodies.
  • The 4 Fs: Find, Filter, Fill, Fire. Most gaps fail the filter, and some valid ones never come back.
  • The trigger is a close back above the gap after a dip into it. The gap is where you look; the reaction is why you act.
  • Stop 2 pips under the gap, target 2R, size from fixed risk. At 2R, roughly a third of trades must win to break even before costs.

Keep it: the body test matters most
Discard it: all three checks must hold
Keep it, but halve the size

Wait: F4 needs a close back above the gap's top
Sell: the gap has failed
Move the gap lower

The close shows price was pushed back out of the gap; a resting order buys whatever happens, including a slice straight through
Closes always lead to winning trades
Resting orders get worse prices
quiz.why: The fill is not the signal. The reaction is the observable evidence, and it is still no guarantee.

lessons.title: Fair Value Gaps — One Full Trade, Start to Finish
lessons.summary: Run the 4 Fs under pressure — the "always fills" trap re-run, a valid trade that still loses, one complete trade with entry, stop, target and size — and practise the buy-or-wait decision until it is automatic.
lessons.html:
Episode 5 gave you the 4 Fs: Find, Filter, Fill, Fire. Rules on a whiteboard are easy. This lesson puts them under pressure. First, the gap from the start of the last lesson, run through the rules instead of a hunch. Then a trade that passes all four Fs and still loses — and why that is fine. Then one full trade, start to finish, with every number written down before the entry.

A quick reminder of the rules, exactly as they stand:

  • Find: three candles; candle 3's low is above candle 1's high. Use the wicks.
  • Filter: middle body at least 2× the average of the previous 10; the move closes above the highest high of the previous 12 candles; the gap is at least 3 pips. All three.
  • Fill: price comes back into the gap within 20 candles. Don't chase.
  • Fire: buy only when a candle dips into the gap and closes back above its top. Stop 2 pips under the gap. Target 2R. A close below the gap first means the gap has failed.

The trap: the gap from the start, re-run

Last lesson opened with a blind buy order resting at the top of an 8.2-pip gap. Price came back, filled it, and kept falling: −10.2 pips at the stop, and 31 pips below the order by the end of the move.

Now walk the same training chart through the rules, one F at a time.

Find: yes. Candle 3's low sits 8.2 pips above candle 1's high. Filter: yes. The middle candle's body is many times the average of the ten before it, it closes above every high of the previous 12 candles, and 8.2 pips is well over the 3-pip minimum. Fill: yes. Price trades back into the gap eight candles later, well inside the 20-candle window.

Fire: no. The candle that enters the gap closes inside it, not above it. Under the rules that is a wait, not a buy. The very next candle closes below the gap. The gap has failed before any reaction appeared, so there is no trade at all.

That is the whole difference between the blind order and the method. Both saw the same gap. Both saw price return to it. Only one of them required price to show something on the way back before money went in.

KEY POINT

The fill tells you price arrived. The close back above the gap tells you price was pushed out again. Only the second is a signal.

A trade that passes all 4 Fs and loses

Now the uncomfortable one. Here is a gap that does everything right. It is found by the wick rule. It passes all three filter checks. Price returns inside 20 candles. A candle dips into the gap and closes back above its top. You buy the close, with the stop 2 pips under the gap — a 12.7-pip stop — and a 2R target above.

Four candles later, the stop is gone. −1R.

Was the trade a mistake? No. Nothing was skipped, nothing was moved, the loss was the size it was planned to be. A valid trade can still lose. That is the point of sizing.

The arithmetic explains why this is survivable. With a 2R target and a 1R stop, one win pays for two losses, so roughly a third of trades need to win just to break even before costs. Put the other way round: a method aiming at 2R can be wrong most of the time and still break even. Those are hypothetical numbers, not a promise about this method, but they tell you what to expect. Losses like this one are not exceptions to the plan. They are the plan, priced in advance.

What would turn this into a real mistake? Any of the things traders do after a loss: moving the stop lower "to give it room", buying again without a fresh reaction, or quietly adding a fourth filter so that this particular chart would have been excluded. All three make your records less true.

One full trade, start to finish

Now the full sequence, on one training chart, with the numbers you would actually write down. EUR/USD, 15-minute.

Find. Candle 1's high is 1.08626. Candle 3's low is 1.08708. The gap is 8.2 pips.

Filter. The middle candle's body is far above 2× the average of the previous 10. The move closes above the highest high of the previous 12 candles. 8.2 pips clears the 3-pip minimum. All three checks pass, so the gap goes on the watch list.

Fill. Price rallies away, then drifts back. Ten candles after the gap formed, a candle dips into it — well inside the 20-candle window. You have not placed an order. You are waiting for a close.

Fire. That candle closes at 1.08738, back above the gap's top. That is the trigger. Entry at the close: 1.08738.

Stop. 2 pips under the gap: 1.08606. That is a 13.2-pip stop.

Target. 2R: 26.4 pips above entry, at 1.09002.

Size. Illustrative account £2,000, risk 1%: £20. £20 ÷ 13.2 pips ≈ £1.52 a pip.

Then you do nothing. The target is reached seven candles later — an hour and three-quarters on the 15-minute chart. Before costs, that is about +£40, or +2R.

Notice what this trade and the losing one have in common: everything you controlled. Same rules, same stop logic, same target, same risk. The outcome was the only thing that changed, and you never controlled that.

COMMON MISTAKE

Learning the wrong lesson from the result. The win does not prove the rules; the loss does not disprove them. Only a large, honestly recorded sample can tell you anything.

Your call: buy or wait?

The rules turn every moment at a gap into one of a small number of decisions. In the episode you get four in a row: a 2.5-pip gap that breaks nothing (skip), an 8.4-pip gap that has just formed (wait for the fill), a close inside the gap (wait), and a close back above (buy). Try the two charts below before you reveal the answers.

Quick answers

Does the gap have to fill completely? No. F3 only asks price to come back into the gap. Many strong moves dip into the top of a gap and leave, and the trigger — a close back above — works the same way whether the dip went one pip in or all the way to the bottom.

What if the reaction candle closes a long way above the gap? The stop is still 2 pips under the gap, so the stop gets wider and the size gets smaller. The risk in money does not change. If the stop becomes so wide that the 2R target sits somewhere absurd, that is a judgement your testing should settle in advance, not on the day.

Can I place a limit order in the gap instead? Not under these rules. A resting order is the blind buy from the start of lesson 5. It fills on the dip whether or not a reaction ever comes.

Does this work for sells? The mirror image applies: candle 1's low above candle 3's high, a close below the lowest low of the previous 12 candles, a close back below the gap to fire, and the stop 2 pips above it. Test it separately; do not assume the results carry over.

Which timeframe? The examples here are 15-minute charts. The rules are written in candles, so they apply on any timeframe, but the 3-pip minimum means much more on a 1-minute chart than on a daily one. Pick one timeframe, test it, and stay on it.

Six mistakes to avoid

  1. Buying the touch. A resting order at the gap buys every slice straight through. Wait for the close.
  2. Two out of three. A gap that fails one filter check has failed. "It nearly passed" is not a category.
  3. Chasing the gap that left. If price never comes back within 20 candles, the trade does not exist.
  4. Waiting through a failure. A close below the gap before a reaction ends it. Do not wait for "a better reaction" lower down.
  5. Touching the trade after entry. Moving the stop, cutting the target short of 2R, or adding size after a dip all change a tested plan into an untested one.
  6. Rewriting the rules after one result. One loss is not evidence, and neither is one win.

How to practise, and the checklist

Practise on historical charts first, then on a demo account. Keep a gap tally sheet with four columns: found → filtered → filled → fired. In the episode's example chart the tally reads 9 → 2 → 1 → 1. Your own tallies will tell you how often your pair and timeframe produce a tradeable gap, and how patient the method requires you to be.

For every trade that reaches F4, log the gap size, the stop in pips, the size you used, the result in R, and one line on anything you were tempted to do differently. Judge the method on the whole log, not on last Tuesday.

PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Find: candle 3's low is above candle 1's high (wicks, not bodies)
  • Filter: middle body ≥ 2× the average of the previous 10
  • Filter: the move closes above the highest high of the previous 12 candles
  • Filter: gap ≥ 3 pips
  • Fill: price is back in the gap within 20 candles of it forming
  • No candle has closed below the gap
  • Fire: a candle has dipped into the gap and closed back above its top
  • Stop 2 pips under the gap; target 2R; size from a fixed risk per trade (e.g. 1%)
  • Logged in the tally sheet and the journal before the next chart

Going deeper

Losing streaks are normal arithmetic. Even in a hypothetical method where a third of trades reach 2R, runs of five or six losses in a row are not rare. At 1% risk per trade, six straight losses cost roughly 6% of the account. That is why risk is fixed and small: the method is meant to survive the bad stretch it will certainly meet, not to be right on every trade.

Costs relative to the stop. The examples are "before costs". A spread of one pip on a 13-pip stop is nearly 8% of your risk on every trade, paid whether you win or lose. That is one reason for the 3-pip minimum gap, and one reason to test with realistic costs before you believe any result.

Why the stop sits under the gap, not under the swing low. The rules place the stop 2 pips under the gap because a close below the gap is exactly what defines failure. Other methods anchor stops to swing lows or swept extremes, which gives a different trade with a different size. Neither is "right"; mixing them trade by trade is wrong.

What the rules leave out. The 4 Fs judge the gap and the reaction. They do not look at the higher-timeframe trend, at which liquidity the displacement took, or at the session. Later episodes add those layers. Adding them is fine — but add them as fixed rules, test them, and compare against the plain 4 Fs, so you know whether each layer earns its place.

THE RULES
  • The fill is not the signal. A close back above the gap after a dip into it is.
  • A close below the gap before a reaction means the gap has failed. No trade.
  • Stop 2 pips under the gap, target 2R, risk fixed per trade. Nothing changes after entry.
  • A valid trade can lose. Judge the method on the full log, never on one result.

Summary

  • Run through the rules, the "always fills" gap passes Find, Filter and Fill, then fails before it ever fires — no trade.
  • A trade can pass all four Fs and still lose. Sizing makes that a planned 1R, and at 2R roughly a third of trades must win to break even before costs.
  • The full trade: gap 1.08626–1.08708, entry 1.08738, stop 1.08606 (13.2 pips), target 2R, about £1.52 a pip on 1% of £2,000.
  • At a gap, the decisions are few: skip, wait for the fill, wait for the close, or buy.
  • Practise with a found → filtered → filled → fired tally and a journal, and judge the method on the whole record.
