lessons.title: Order Blocks Explained — Which Ones Are Worth Watching
lessons.summary: Mark bullish and bearish order blocks with one written rule, put every candidate through the four checks (break, force, gap, fresh), and act on the reaction rather than the touch.
lessons.html:
You have probably heard the rule. Find the last down candle before a big move up. That is an order block. When price comes back to it, it bounces.

So you wait. Price comes back, right into the box, and closes straight through it.

Apply that rule to a whole chart and you find a box under almost every swing. A few of them held beautifully: price came back, touched them and launched again. Some were sliced straight through. Most did nothing at all. From the boxes alone, you cannot tell which were which.

This lesson follows Episode 7 and answers the two questions the film asks. Which order blocks are worth watching? And when price gets back to one, what should you actually be looking for?

The "last down candle" rule, and why it is incomplete

The popular rule is not wrong. It is incomplete. "Last down candle before a move up" describes a location, not a quality. Every swing low on every chart has a last down candle somewhere near it, because that is how swing lows are made: price falls, then stops falling. If the rule were enough, every swing low would be an order block, and the word would mean nothing.

What separates a useful zone from wallpaper is everything that happens after the candle: how far the move went, how fast it went, what it left behind, and whether price has already been back. Those are things you can check on the chart, in the moment, without guessing anyone's intentions. That is what the rest of this lesson builds.

What an order block is — observably and in framework language

Start with what the chart actually shows. Price was drifting lower. Then, in one or two candles, it turned and left that area fast — fast enough to close above the last swing high. The last down candle before that move is where the turn happened. That candle is what Smart Money Concepts calls an order block.

There are two descriptions of the same candle:

  • Observable: a zone price left quickly, just before it broke structure.
  • Framework: an order block.

Why the name? The usual explanation is that large traders built a big position there, and some of their orders may still be waiting if price comes back. Here is the honest part. On spot forex you cannot see those orders. There is no central order book to check. Any picture of "orders sitting in the zone" is illustrative. Treat that explanation as the framework's story, not a measurement.

What you can check is the candle, the move that left it, and what price does when it returns. Everything in this lesson is built on those three things.

KEY POINT

Price first. Framework second. The candle and the move are facts; the orders are a story.

Our definition, written down

Definitions vary between educators, so here is ours, written down, exactly as the film uses it.

  • A bullish order block is the last candle that closed down, before a strong move up that closes above a swing high. That close is a break of structure or a change of character, as defined in Episode 1.
  • A bearish order block is the mirror: the last candle that closed up, before a strong move down that closes below a swing low.
  • The zone is the whole candle, from its high to its low, wicks included.

Swings use the same convention as the rest of the series: a swing high is a candle whose high is above the two candles either side of it, and it is only confirmed two candles later. A wick above the swing high is not a break. A close is.

Why the whole candle

Some traders use only the body. Some draw several candles together. Some refine the zone on a lower timeframe. None of those is wrong; they are choices. Ours is the whole candle, every time, so the rule never moves. A rule that changes shape from trade to trade is not a rule. It is a way of making the chart agree with you after the event.

The four checks: break, force, gap, fresh

Go back to the chart with a box under every swing. Now put each box through four checks, in order. A candidate that fails any one of them is not worth watching.

  1. Break. Did the move away from the candle close above a swing high (for a bullish block)? If it did not break anything, it is just a down candle before an up candle.
  2. Force. Was there displacement? In this series, displacement means at least one candle in the move with a body at least twice the average body of the previous ten candles. This is the same test used in Episodes 1 and 5.
  3. Gap. Did the move leave a fair value gap — a gap between the first candle's high and the third candle's low? A gap is the footprint of a fast move, and it often sits right next to the order block.
  4. Fresh. Has price already been back to it? We count only the first return. Once a zone has been traded into, it has been used.

Look at candidate B carefully, because it is the box from the start of the film. Its move away did close above the swing highs, so it passed the break check. But the climb was made of ordinary candles, none of them with a body twice the recent average. The move was steady, not fast. Under our rules it never qualified, and when price came back it closed straight through.

That does not mean candidate C will work. It means C is worth watching. Which is a much smaller job.

KEY POINT

Worth watching is not the same as will work. The four checks decide where you look, not what happens next.

Liquidity first: the sweep

Many SMC traders look for one more thing, and it ties back to Episodes 3 and 4. Did the move that created the order block start with a sweep?

In the next chart, price trades below an old low, closes back above it, and then launches. The last down candle before the launch is the order block, and it sits right on top of the sweep. In SMC language, sell-side liquidity was taken, structure broke, and the order block marks where it turned. Observably: a wick below an obvious low, a close back above it, then a large-bodied move that closed above the last swing high.

We do not make the sweep compulsory. But when the order block sits on a sweep, the sequence is complete: taken, turned, broke.

Continuation or reversal

Order blocks appear in two places, and it helps to know which one you are looking at.

  • In a trend (continuation). In an uptrend, price pulls back, then breaks the next high. The last down candle of that pullback is a continuation order block. It is tied to a break of structure. It goes with the trend you already have.
  • At a turn (reversal). Price has been falling, then closes above the last lower high. The last down candle before that close is a reversal order block. It is tied to a change of character. It is a bet that the trend has changed, which is why the higher timeframe matters so much here.

Same definition, different job. The bearish version below is a reversal block: an uptrend, then a fast drop that closes below the last higher low.

The return: reaction or failure

Now the part most people skip. What happens when price comes back?

The first return into the zone is what the framework calls mitigation. The idea is that any orders left behind get filled. Observably, all we can say is that price traded back into the box. That is the observable line and the framework label again, side by side.

A touch is a question, not an answer. Two things can happen:

  • Reaction. Price trades into the box and closes back above its top (for a bullish block). The zone held, for now.
  • Failure. Price closes below the bottom of the box. The zone has failed. No debate, and no redrawing it lower.

Some traders also watch the midpoint of the zone. A close below halfway is an early warning. We note it; we do not require it.

This is the same idea as the fill in Episode 6. The zone is where you look. The reaction is why you act.

COMMON MISTAKE

Buying the first touch. The touch is also where failing order blocks fail. Wait for the candle to close back out of the zone.

One trade, start to finish

Here is the same chart, run start to finish, exactly as in the film.

  1. The sweep. Price traded below the old low at 1.0859 and closed back above it.
  2. The four checks. The move closed above the last swing high (break). Its candles had bodies of 26 and 32 pips against a recent average of well under ten (force). It left a fair value gap between 1.0876 and 1.0888 (gap). Price had not been back (fresh). Four checks, four ticks.
  3. The return. Price drifted back over the next several hours. The first candle into the zone closed inside it — a touch. The next closed back above it at 1.0884 — the reaction.
  4. The plan. Entry at that close, 1.0884. Stop two pips below the bottom of the zone, at 1.0852, because if price closes down there the idea is wrong. Risk: 32 pips.
  5. The target. The next obvious pool of liquidity above: the equal highs at 1.0960, buy-side liquidity in SMC language. That is 76 pips away, about 2.4R. The rule is that the target must be at least 2R away, or there is no trade.
  6. The size. Position size comes from the stop, not from confidence. Decide the risk — say 1% of the account — and divide it by the stop distance. A wider zone means a smaller position, not a bigger loss.

This is the clean version. Lesson 8 shows the one that matters more: a block that passes every check, gives a reaction, and still stops you out.

Going deeper

Why force is measured, not felt. "Strong move" is the phrase every order block definition uses and almost none defines. Without a number, every move looks strong in hindsight if it went somewhere. The body-versus-ten-candle-average test is crude, but it is the same test every time, it uses only candles that already existed, and it can be coded. On a quiet Asian-session chart a 12-pip body might qualify; during London the same body might not. That is intended: displacement is relative to what the market was doing just before.

Freshness is about crowding as much as orders. On the framework's story, the first return fills what was left behind, so the second has less to fill. There is also a plainer reason: once price has reacted from a zone, it has become an obvious level that many traders will have drawn, with stops just beyond it. By the logic of Episode 4, an obvious level with stops beyond it is a pool, not a floor.

Continuation blocks need less from the higher timeframe than reversal blocks. A continuation block goes with structure that already exists. A reversal block asks you to believe the first CHOCH is the start of something. If the higher timeframe is still clearly falling, a bullish reversal block on H1 is a bounce inside a downtrend until proven otherwise. Episodes 9 and 10 build that check properly.

What to count when you test. Of the candidates that pass all four checks on your pair and timeframe, how many produce a reaction on the first return? Of those, how many reach 2R before a close through the zone? Write down every candidate before price returns. Candidates marked afterwards are always better than the ones you would actually have traded.

THE RULES
  • Bullish OB: the last down-close candle before a move that closes above a swing high. Bearish: the mirror.
  • Zone: the whole candle, high to low, wicks included. Every time.
  • Four checks before it is worth watching: break (a close beyond a swing), force (a body at least 2× the average of the previous 10), gap (an FVG in the move), fresh (first return only).
  • A touch is not a signal. Act only on a reaction: a candle that closes back out of the zone.
  • A close through the far side means the zone has failed. Do not redraw it.
  • Stop two pips beyond the zone; target the next obvious pool; at least 2R or no trade; size from 1% risk divided by the stop.

Summary

  • "Last down candle before a move up" is a location, not a quality. On its own it marks almost every swing.
  • Our definition: the last down-close candle before a move that closes above a swing high. The zone is the whole candle.
  • Four checks decide which candidates are worth watching: break, force, gap, fresh. Most boxes fail at least one.
  • A sweep before the order block completes the sequence, but it is not compulsory. Continuation blocks follow a BOS; reversal blocks follow a CHOCH.
  • On the return, the zone is where you look and the reaction close is why you act. A close through the far side ends it.

quiz.q: Under our definition, which candle is a bullish order block?
options: The largest green candle in the rally
The last down-close candle before a move that closes above a swing high
Any red candle at a swing low
The first candle that closes above the swing high
quiz.why: The block is the last down-close candle before the move, and the move must close above a swing high. A red candle at a low with no break is just a red candle.

quiz.q: A candidate's move closed above the swing high and left a fair value gap, but no candle in it had a body at least twice the average of the previous ten. Which check did it fail?
options: Break
Gap
Force
Fresh
quiz.why: Force is the displacement test: at least one body twice the recent average. An ordinary, steady climb fails it even if it breaks structure.

quiz.q: In the 'three candidates' chart, why was candidate A not an order block?
options: Its rally stalled under the swing high, so nothing broke
It was too small
It had already been used
It was not on a sweep
quiz.why: No close beyond a swing means no break, and under our rules no break means no order block, however sharp the rally looked.

quiz.q: Price trades into a fresh bullish order block and the candle closes inside the zone. What do you do?
options: Buy at the close
Wait for a candle that closes back above the zone
Redraw the zone lower
Short it, because the zone is failing
quiz.why: A touch is a question, not an answer. The reaction — a close back out of the zone — is the reason to act. A close inside is neither a reaction nor a failure.

quiz.q: In the worked example, why is the stop two pips below the bottom of the zone rather than inside it?
options: To make the R multiple look bigger
Because the broker requires it
Because a close below the zone means the idea is wrong, so the stop belongs beyond it
Because the midpoint is irrelevant
quiz.why: The zone is the reason for the trade. If price closes beyond its far side the zone has failed, so the stop sits just beyond that point — not inside the zone where an ordinary wick can reach it.

lessons.title: Order Blocks — When They Fail, and Breaker Blocks
lessons.summary: Take a loss on a perfectly valid order block without breaking your rules, recognise the charts with nothing to trade, read a failed zone as a possible breaker, and run the full order block checklist.
lessons.html:
Lesson 7 gave you the four checks — break, force, gap, fresh — and one trade that worked. This lesson, like Episode 8, starts with the trade that matters more: an order block that passes every check, gives a reaction, and still stops you out.

If the only examples you ever study are winners, you will build a method that cannot survive its first loss. So this lesson spends its time on the uncomfortable parts. What a loss looks like when you have done everything right. Why the 2R target rule exists. Which charts have nothing to trade. What happens to a zone after it fails. And the handful of mistakes that turn a small, planned loss into a large, unplanned one.

Where we pick up

A quick reminder of the convention, because everything below depends on it:

  • A bullish order block is the last down-close candle before a move that closes above a swing high. A bearish block is the mirror.
  • The zone is the whole candle, high to low, wicks included.
  • It is worth watching only if it passes four checks: break (a close beyond a swing), force (a body at least twice the average of the previous ten), gap (a fair value gap in the move) and fresh (first return only).
  • On the return, you act on the reaction: a candle that closes back out of the zone. A close through the far side means the zone has failed.

As always: price first, framework second. The candle, the move and the return are on the chart. Any story about orders resting inside the zone is the framework's explanation, and on spot forex there is no central order book to confirm it.

When it fails — and why 2R matters

Pound-dollar, one-hour chart. Same checklist as the winning trade in Lesson 7.

Price swept an old low and closed back above it. Two large-bodied candles then closed above the last swing high (break, force). They left a fair value gap (gap). Price had not been back (fresh). All four pass.

Price returned, the first candle closed inside the zone — a touch — and the next closed back above it. A reaction. Entry at that close, stop two pips under the zone, target the equal highs above, a little over 2R away.

Three candles later, price closed below the zone. Stopped out. A full 1R loss.

Nothing was wrong with the order block. Nothing was wrong with the entry. This is simply what a loss looks like when you have done everything right. The four checks decide where you look, and the reaction decides when you act. Neither of them decides what price does next.

KEY POINT

A valid order block can fail. The plan exists for that moment, not for the winners.

The arithmetic behind the 2R rule

Here is why the minimum target matters. If every win is at least 2R and every loss is 1R, then one win pays for two losses:

  • 1 win × 2R = +2R
  • 2 losses × 1R = −2R

So, before costs, you need to be right about one time in three just to break even. Spread, commission and slippage push that number up a little; a target below 2R pushes it up a lot. At 1R targets you would need to be right half the time before costs, with no margin for anything.

That is not a promise of anything. It is arithmetic. It says nothing about how often order blocks work on your pair — only your own records can tell you that. It is simply the reason the plan has a minimum target at all, and why a setup that cannot reach 2R is not a setup.

When there is nothing to trade

Just as useful as the trade is knowing when there is no trade. The film shows two cases.

No break. A sharp move up from a down candle — large bodies, even a gap — that stops short of the last swing high. Nothing broke. Under our rules, that down candle is not an order block at all. It is just a down candle, however dramatic the move after it looked.

Used. A real order block that passed all four checks, and that price has already traded back into once. The first return was the one that counted. Second time around, the zone is used, and we let it go.

Skipping is a decision. Most of the job is deciding what to leave alone, and a method that always finds something to trade is not filtering anything.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating "no trade" as wasted time. A chart you correctly pass on costs nothing. A chart you force a trade on costs at least 1R.

Breaker blocks

So what happens to an order block after it fails? Some SMC traders keep watching it — from the other side.

Go back to the failed pound-dollar block. Observably, price closed through the zone and kept falling. Later, it came back up to the same area from below, traded into it, and a candle closed back under it. Price turned lower again.

In framework language, a failed order block that gets retested from the other side is often called a breaker block. Definitions vary: some educators only use the term when the failed block was formed by a sweep, or when the break that defeated it was itself a change of character. We use the plain version and say so.

It is the same idea you met with levels in Episode 4. A line that breaks can flip from floor to ceiling. The breaker is a zone version of that flip. And just as with any zone, the reaction decides, not the label. A breaker is a place to look. If you treat it as a short, it needs the same things as any order block trade: a close back out of the zone (here, a close back below it), a stop beyond the far side, a target at the next pool and at least 2R.

There is also a quieter lesson in this chart. The trader who took the loss and moved on was free to watch the zone from the other side. The trader who redrew the box lower and held on was still long.

Order blocks, fair value gaps and supply and demand

Three terms that get mixed up.

  • The order block is the candle before the move.
  • The fair value gap is the hole inside the move: the gap between the first candle's high and the third candle's low.
  • A supply or demand zone is the older idea behind both. Usually wider, usually drawn by eye around the whole base the move came from.

Because the displacement candle that leaves the gap starts right at the order block, the two usually sit next to each other. When both line up, many SMC traders treat the combined area as the place to watch: order block plus fair value gap. An order block is, in effect, a narrower, rule-based version of a demand zone.

Timeframes: a 4H block is not a 5M block

An order block on a five-minute chart and one on a four-hour chart are not the same size of idea. One four-hour candle contains 48 five-minute candles. A four-hour order block can therefore contain dozens of possible five-minute order blocks.

  • 4H zones are wider and visible to far more traders. The stop is wide, so the position is small.
  • 5M zones are tighter and give a smaller stop, but they are far more numerous, and most of them mean little on their own.

The small one often sits inside the big one. Episodes 9 and 10 are about using both at once: the higher timeframe for the bias and the zone, the lower for the trigger.

Quick answers

Body or wick? We use the whole candle, wicks included. Body-only zones are tighter, and price will trade through them more often. Pick one and never switch mid-trade.

How long does an order block stay valid? Until it has been traded into once, or until price closes through it. Some traders also drop zones after a set number of candles. That is a reasonable extra filter, not a requirement.

What if the zone is huge? Then so is the stop. If the stop is too wide for a 2R target to land at a sensible pool, it is not a trade. A big zone on a high timeframe is often refined on a lower one.

Do order blocks prove institutions are buying? No. They show where price turned and left quickly. Who was behind that move is not something a candle can tell you.

Do they work on every pair? The definition works on any chart. Whether it is useful on a given pair is something you find out by testing it there, not by assuming.

Your turn

The drill below is the film's interactive example. Three down candles are marked A, B and C. Decide which one is the order block under our rules before you reveal.

Five order block mistakes, and a bonus

  1. Calling every down candle an order block. No break, no order block.
  2. Buying the first touch without waiting for a reaction. The touch is where order blocks fail, too.
  3. Putting the stop inside the zone. If the zone is the reason for the trade, the stop goes beyond it.
  4. Using a zone that has already been traded into. First return only.
  5. Buying a bullish order block while the higher timeframe is clearly falling. That is a bounce inside a downtrend until proven otherwise — which is exactly what Episodes 9 and 10 deal with.

And the bonus: redrawing the zone lower after price closes through it. A failed zone has failed. Moving the box is how a small loss becomes a big one.

Going deeper

Losses cluster. If the break-even rate at 2R is one in three before costs, then even a method that is right more often than that will regularly produce runs of four, five or six losses in a row. That is ordinary variance, not proof that the method is broken. It is why risk per trade is fixed at a small fraction — 1% in this series — and why position size always comes from the stop distance. Judge the method on a large sample, not the last week.

Why failed zones can be useful. A zone that should have held, by every rule you wrote, and did not, tells you something about the balance of buying and selling at that moment. The breaker idea turns that into a location to watch. It is not more reliable than an ordinary order block, and it needs the same reaction close before you act on it.

Crowding and the stop buffer. A textbook order block on a popular pair is drawn by many traders, with entries at the edge and stops just beyond. By the logic of Episode 4, that is itself a pool. It is one reason zones sometimes fail by a few pips and then turn. The two-pip buffer is a fixed, honest convention; widen it only if your own records show a reason, and size down when you do.

Testing your version. Mark every candidate on a month of one-hour charts on a demo account. Run the four checks. Write down, for each one, whether the first return gave a reaction, whether the reaction reached 2R before a close through the zone, and what happened if it failed. Then do the same for the failed zones as possible breakers. The list will teach you more than any single trade.

THE RULES
  • A valid order block can still fail. The stop is part of the plan, not a verdict on the method.
  • Target at least 2R, or no trade. At 2R, one win pays for two losses before costs.
  • No break, no order block. A zone already traded into once is used: skip it.
  • A close through the far side means failed. Never redraw the zone.
  • A failed zone may be watched from the other side as a breaker; the reaction decides, not the label.
  • Risk 1% per trade; size = risk ÷ stop distance.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Break: did the move close beyond a swing high (low for bearish)?
  • Force: is there a body at least twice the average of the previous ten candles?
  • Gap: did the move leave a fair value gap?
  • Fresh: is this the first return to the zone?
  • Reaction: has a candle closed back out of the zone?
  • Plan: stop two pips beyond the zone, target the next obvious pool, at least 2R — or no trade
  • Size: 1% risk divided by the stop distance
  • Higher timeframe: not clearly against the trade

Summary

  • An order block can pass every check, give a reaction, and still fail. That loss is part of the method, not a fault in it.
  • The 2R minimum is arithmetic: one win pays for two losses, so the break-even rate before costs is about one in three.
  • No break means no order block, and a zone already traded into is used. Skipping is a decision.
  • A failed zone retested from the other side is what the framework calls a breaker block. The reaction decides, not the label.
  • The order block is the candle before the move; the fair value gap is the hole inside it; a demand zone is the wider, by-eye version of the same idea.

quiz.q: A block passes all four checks, gives a reaction close, and you are stopped out three candles later. What does that tell you?
options: The four checks are useless
You should have drawn the zone wider
Nothing was necessarily wrong — a valid order block can fail, and the stop is part of the plan
You should redraw the zone lower and re-enter
quiz.why: The checks decide where you look and the reaction decides when you act. Neither guarantees the outcome. A 1R loss on a valid setup is what doing everything right sometimes looks like.

quiz.q: Every win is 2R and every loss is 1R. Before costs, roughly how often must you be right to break even?
options: One time in two
One time in three
One time in four
Nine times in ten
quiz.why: One 2R win pays for two 1R losses, so one in three breaks even before costs. Costs push it slightly higher.

quiz.q: A sharp rally leaves a fair value gap but stops short of the last swing high. Under our rules the down candle before it is…
options: An order block
A breaker block
Not an order block — no break
A used order block
quiz.why: No close beyond a swing means no break, and no break means no order block, however strong the move looked.

quiz.q: Which best describes a breaker block in this course?
options: Any order block on the first return
A failed order block that price later retests from the other side
The fair value gap inside a displacement
A demand zone drawn by eye
quiz.why: Observably: a zone that price closed through, later revisited from the other side. The framework calls it a breaker; the reaction still decides whether it matters.

quiz.q: Price closes through the bottom of your bullish order block. What do you do with the zone?
options: Redraw it lower to include the new low
Treat it as failed; it may be watched later from the other side
Add to the position at a better price
Switch to a body-only zone so it still holds
quiz.why: Failed means failed. Redrawing or switching conventions mid-trade is how a planned 1R loss becomes an unplanned large one.

lessons.title: Top-Down Analysis — Three Timeframes, Three Questions
lessons.summary: Use the 4H for direction, the 1H for location and the draw, and the 5M for timing, in that order, so a small chart never overrules a big one.
lessons.html:
Five-minute chart, EUR/USD. Price sweeps a low, closes above the last lower high, and pulls back into a fresh order block. Every box from the last eight episodes is ticked. You buy, with the stop under the sweep low. Then a candle closes straight through the zone and price keeps falling.

Now zoom out to the four-hour chart. Same candles. Price was in a clean downtrend, sitting just underneath a bearish order block. That perfect setup was a small bounce inside a falling market.

The five-minute chart was not wrong. It was answering the wrong question. This lesson is about asking the right questions, on the right charts, in the right order.

Why one chart isn't enough

You saw this in episode 1. The same eight hours can be bullish on the four-hour chart and bearish on the five-minute. Both are true at the same time, because each chart is answering a different question about a different amount of price.

That is not a contradiction to be resolved. It is a division of labour to be organised. The mistake is asking one chart to answer every question, and the usual version of that mistake is asking the smallest chart, because it is the one that moves while you watch.

Top-down analysis simply means asking the questions in order: biggest picture first, smallest last.

Three timeframes, three questions

In this series we use three timeframes, and each one has exactly one job.

Timeframe Question What it may not do
4H Direction — which way is the bigger structure pointing? Time an entry
1H Location — where would we want to be involved, and where is price likely to be drawn? Change the 4H bias
5M Timing — is something happening right now, at that location, that we can act on? Create a trade the 1H has not located

Definitions vary. Other traders use the daily, the fifteen-minute and the one-minute, or the one-hour, fifteen-minute and one-minute. That is fine. What matters is the ratio — each chart a big step down from the one above — and that each chart keeps its own job.

Over all of it sits one rule:

KEY POINT

The higher timeframe decides. The lower timeframe executes. A five-minute chart never overrules a four-hour one.

Step 1: Direction (4H)

Start on the four-hour and use exactly what you learned in episodes 1 and 2. A swing high is a candle whose high is above the highs of the two candles either side of it, and it is only confirmed two candles later. A break counts only on a close. A BOS is a close through a swing in the direction of the trend; a CHOCH is the first close through the last swing against it.

The bias is set by the last break by close. If the last break was a close above a swing high, inside a sequence of higher highs and higher lows, the bias is bullish. It stays bullish for as long as the higher low that produced that break holds.

Use the external structure. On the four-hour, the bias comes from the big swings that define the move. The small wiggles inside a pullback are internal structure; at this size they are noise, and they belong to the lower timeframes. Let them stay there.

The mirror is the same rule upside down: lower highs, lower lows, last break a close below a swing low, and the bias is bearish until a close above the lower high that produced it.

And then there is the chart most people trade anyway: overlapping swings, breaks in both directions, no clear sequence. No bias means no trade on that pair. Not a smaller trade. No trade. Check another pair instead.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating the bias as a prediction. It is a working assumption with a written line that ends it. "Bullish while the 4H closes above 1.0924" is a bias. "It's going up" is a hope.

Premium and discount

Knowing the direction is not enough. You also need to know whether price is cheap or expensive inside the current move.

Take the four-hour leg that made the last break, from its swing low to its swing high. That is the dealing range. Halfway up is the 50% line — in framework language, equilibrium. Above it is premium; below it is discount.

Price first, framework second. Observably, the line is just the halfway point of the last leg. In SMC language it splits expensive from cheap. Same line, two descriptions — and only the first is a fact about the chart.

The rule we use is simple:

  • Bullish bias → longs only in discount.
  • Bearish bias → shorts only in premium.

Why? Buying in the lower half of a range you think is going up leaves more room to the top, and puts your stop closer to the low that ends the idea. Compare two longs in the range above, both targeting the 1.1040 high with a stop under the 1.0840 low. Bought at 1.1000, in premium, the stop is 160 pips away and the target 40: a quarter of an R. Bought at 1.0910, in discount, the stop is 70 pips and the target 130: nearly 2R. That is the shape of the trade, not a promise about its outcome.

You will also hear about the optimal trade entry, OTE: usually the area between about 62% and 79% of the way back down the leg. It is a framework name and the exact numbers vary between educators. We show it. We do not require it.

Step 2: Location (1H)

Now drop to the one-hour chart. Same dates, same prices; each four-hour candle is now four one-hour candles.

You are looking for one thing: a zone inside the four-hour discount that passes the checks from episodes 5 to 8. An order block that passes Break, Force, Gap and Fresh; a fair value gap left by displacement; or, best of all, both together — an order block with a gap just above it.

In SMC language that is your point of interest. Observably, it is the place you have decided, in advance, to pay attention to. Nothing more. A zone up in premium does not count for longs, however good it looks. Wrong half of the range.

Then mark the draw: the next obvious pool of liquidity in the direction of the bias. With a bullish bias that is usually the four-hour swing high — buy-side liquidity resting above the top of the dealing range. Remember that spot FX has no central order book, so "liquidity above the high" is a description of where stops are commonly placed, not a ledger you can see.

Before the five-minute chart even opens, you now know three things: which way, where, and roughly how far.

Write down what ends the location too. If a one-hour candle closes below the zone, the location has failed and there is nothing to look for on the five-minute. And then you wait. Price might take hours or days to reach your zone. It might never get there. That is fine — you have not risked anything yet.

Step 3: Timing (5M)

Price reaches the one-hour zone. Now, and only now, open the five-minute chart.

What you want is the pattern from episodes 3 and 4: a sweep, then a shift.

  1. Sweep. Price trades below a five-minute low and closes back above it. Observably: a wick through a level and a close back inside. In framework language: sell-side liquidity taken.
  2. Shift. A strong candle closes above the last five-minute lower high — a CHOCH — with displacement: a body at least twice the average body of the last ten candles.
  3. Return. That move leaves its own small order block and fair value gap. When price comes back into them and closes back above, that is the trigger.

The stop goes 2 pips below the five-minute sweep low. The target is the draw you marked on the one-hour. And you only take it if the target is at least 2R away.

Timing also has a clock. In forex the five-minute chart is most worth watching when London and New York are open. Our windows are 07:00–11:00 and 12:00–16:00, London time. That is our choice, written down; yours can differ, but it should be written down too. A sweep and shift at three in the morning in a thin Asian session is still information. It just is not our trigger.

Now compare that with buying straight off the one-hour zone, stop under the whole zone. Same target. In the drill the 1H zone runs from 1.0810 to 1.0862. Buy at its top with the stop 2 pips under its low and you risk 54 pips to make 88: about 1.6R, which fails the 2R rule. The 5M trigger risks 32 pips to make 78: about 2.4R. With the same 1% of the account at risk, the wide stop also buys a much smaller position. On a four-hour zone the difference is several times larger.

KEY POINT

The stop comes from the small chart. The target comes from the big one. That is where the room in a top-down trade comes from.

Going deeper

Why the ratios matter. 4H to 1H is 4:1; 1H to 5M is 12:1. At ratios like these the internal structure of one chart becomes roughly the swing structure of the next one down, so the same swing and break rules work at every level. Stacks that are too close together (1H, 30M, 15M) mostly show you the same thing three times; stacks too far apart (daily straight to 1M) leave a gap where the location question should be answered.

When the bias was made by a CHOCH. If the last 4H break was a CHOCH — the first close against the old trend — the new bias exists, but its dealing range is young. Some traders wait for one BOS in the new direction before trusting it. That is a reasonable, written variant; switching between the two depending on which gives you a trade today is not.

Which leg makes the dealing range? Use the leg that produced the last break by close, from its swing low to its swing high (for a bullish bias). When a new BOS prints, the range is redrawn. If you find yourself redrawing the range to put price into discount, you are shopping, not analysing.

Failure conditions, in order. The 1H location fails on a 1H close through the zone. The 5M trade fails on the stop. The 4H bias fails on a 4H close through the defining swing. Each has its own line, and each is written before the trade.

Where top-down does not help. Around big scheduled news, price can move through any zone on any timeframe. The structure is real; the reason for the move is different. Many traders stand aside, and episode 10 comes back to this.

THE RULES
  • 4H answers direction from external structure: the last break by close. No bias, no trade on that pair.
  • Longs only in 4H discount with a bullish bias; shorts only in 4H premium with a bearish bias.
  • 1H answers location: a zone in the right half that passes Break, Force, Gap, Fresh — plus the draw.
  • 5M answers timing, only once price is at the 1H zone: sweep, shift with displacement, return with a reaction close.
  • Stop 2 pips beyond the 5M sweep extreme; target the draw; at least 2R or no trade.
  • 5M triggers only inside the written windows: 07:00–11:00 and 12:00–16:00 London time.

Summary

  • Each timeframe has one question: 4H direction, 1H location and draw, 5M timing.
  • The bias is the last 4H break by close, and it comes with a written line that ends it.
  • The dealing range splits the last leg into premium and discount; trade with the bias from the right half.
  • The 5M trigger is sweep, shift, return — inside the 1H zone and inside your session windows.
  • The stop comes from the small chart; the target comes from the big one.

quiz.q: In this series, what question does the 1H chart answer?
options: Direction
Location and the draw
Timing
Position size
quiz.why: 4H answers direction, 1H answers location (and where price is likely drawn), 5M answers timing.

quiz.q: The 4H has made higher highs and higher lows; the last break was a close above a swing high. When does the bullish bias end?
options: When the 5M makes a CHOCH down
When a 4H candle wicks below the defining higher low
When a 4H candle closes below the higher low that produced the break
When price enters premium
quiz.why: Breaks count on closes, and the bias is the 4H's job. A 5M CHOCH or a wick does not end it.

quiz.q: The dealing range runs from 1.0840 to 1.1040 with a bullish bias. Price is at 1.0990 and a clean 5M sweep and shift appears. What does the method say?
options: Buy — the 5M setup is clean
No long — price is in premium, above the 1.0940 midpoint
Sell — premium means short
Buy half size
quiz.why: With a bullish bias we only look for longs in discount. Premium is the wrong half, however good the 5M looks; it is not a reason to go short against the bias.

quiz.q: A perfect 5M sweep and shift prints at 03:00 London time inside your 1H zone. Under the written windows, what is it?
options: A trigger
Information, but not our trigger
A reason to widen the stop
A new 4H bias
quiz.why: Our windows are 07:00–11:00 and 12:00–16:00 London time. Outside them a pattern is still information, but not a trigger.

quiz.q: Why does a 5M trigger usually give more R than buying straight off the 1H zone with the same target?
options: The 5M win rate is higher
The stop comes from the small chart, so it is tighter for the same target
The target is further away on the 5M
It does not; R is the same
quiz.why: Same target, tighter stop under the 5M sweep: more R per unit of risk. Nothing here says it wins more often.

lessons.title: When Timeframes Disagree — The Routine, the Conflicts and the Loss
lessons.summary: Run the whole top-down process as a pre-London routine, decide what to do when the 4H, 1H and 5M disagree, and read a failed trade without blaming the plan.
lessons.html:
Episode 9 gave you the three questions: direction on the four-hour, location on the one-hour, timing on the five-minute. This lesson puts them to work. First the whole move in one go, then a routine you can run every morning, then the part most traders get wrong — what to do when the charts disagree. And because a method you only see winning is a method you do not understand yet, we finish the worked example with a full loss.

One price, three timeframes

In the film the showpiece is a single continuous zoom. It is worth walking through slowly, because the point of it is that there is only one price.

Four-hour. Bullish structure: the last break was a close above a swing high. Take the leg that made that break, from its swing low to its swing high — the dealing range — and draw its 50% line. Price is pulling back into the lower half, into discount.

One-hour. Each four-hour candle opens into four one-hour candles. Same open, same high, same low, same close, just with the inside shown. Inside the discount half there is a zone that passes the checks from episodes 5 to 8: an order block with a fair value gap just above it. Above everything sits the four-hour high — the draw.

Five-minute. Each one-hour candle opens into twelve five-minute candles. Price reaches the one-hour zone. A five-minute low is swept, a strong candle closes above the last five-minute lower high, price returns into the small gap that move left, and closes back up. Sweep, shift, return, trigger.

And back out. The five-minute entry, the one-hour zone, the four-hour target. One trade, one story, three charts. Every candle on the smaller charts adds up exactly to the candle above it — this is not three opinions about the market, it is one market seen at three magnifications.

KEY POINT

There is only one price. Timeframes do not disagree about what happened; they describe different amounts of it.

The outcome

In the film's example, price works higher from the trigger and reaches the four-hour high later that session.

The management is deliberately boring. No moving the stop to break-even because it feels safer. No taking half off because you are nervous. No widening the target because it is going well. Entry, stop, target — the plan you wrote before you clicked. If you want a different management rule, that is a legitimate choice, but it is made in advance and tested, never improvised mid-trade.

That is the version where everything lines up. The rest of this lesson is about the versions where it does not.

The pre-London routine

Here is what top-down looks like as a routine, done before London opens.

  1. The four-hour. Write the bias in one word, and the price that would end it. "EUR/USD 4H: bullish. Ends on a 4H close below 1.0924."
  2. The one-hour. Mark the dealing range, the halfway line, and any zone in the right half that passes the checks. Then mark the draw.
  3. The alert. Set a price alert at the edge of the zone, and close the charts.

You do not need to watch price drift for hours. When the alert goes off, then — and only then — you open the five-minute chart. The alert opens the five-minute. Nothing else does. That one habit removes most of the trades people take out of boredom, because boredom never gets the chance to look at a five-minute chart.

COMMON MISTAKE

Opening the five-minute "just to see what it's doing". A chart you have no reason to look at will still give you reasons to trade.

When timeframes disagree

Four-hour bullish. One-hour falling, making lower highs. Is that a conflict?

Usually not. A falling one-hour chart inside a rising four-hour chart is very often just the pullback. It is how price gets back into discount. You do not fight it, and you do not short it because the one-hour "looks bearish". You wait for it to finish — at your zone, with a five-minute sweep and shift.

Now three cases that are genuine conflicts, and the answer to each.

Four-hour bullish, but price is up in premium. No long. However good the five-minute setup looks. The trend being up does not make the top of the range a good place to buy; it makes the bottom of the range the place you are waiting for.

Five-minute shift, but nowhere near a one-hour zone. No trade. A shift in the middle of nowhere is just noise with a label. The five-minute chart prints CHOCHs all day; it is the location that makes one of them worth acting on.

Four-hour bearish, one-hour rising, price climbing into premium. Same idea, upside down. The rally is how price gets expensive enough to short. Wait for it to reach a zone in premium, then look for the five-minute sweep of a high and a shift down.

Most of the time, the three charts do not line up. That is normal. You are not looking for a trade every day. You are looking for the days they agree.

KEY POINT

The higher timeframe decides, the lower timeframe executes. A disagreement is resolved by waiting, never by letting the smaller chart overrule the bigger one.

When it fails

GBP/USD. Four-hour bullish. Price in discount. A one-hour order block with a gap. On the five-minute, a sweep of a low and a displaced close above the last lower high, then a return and a reaction close. Stop 2 pips under the sweep low; target the four-hour high, more than 2R away. Everything aligned.

Price chops around the entry for an hour, then closes through the five-minute sweep low. Stopped. One R.

Then, a few hours later, the four-hour candle closes below the higher low that defined the bias. In framework language that is a CHOCH: the bullish story is over.

Notice the order. The five-minute stop came first. The four-hour close came later. The small chart got you out before the big chart confirmed the change. The plan was not broken. The market changed its mind, and the stop is what told you. That is the job the stop is there to do.

And the arithmetic is the same as in the order-block episodes. With targets of at least 2R, one win pays for two losses. Before costs, that is a break-even rate of about one in three. That is arithmetic, not a forecast: nothing in this lesson tells you how often this process wins on your pair, and only your own records can.

Quick answers

What if the bias flips while I'm in a trade? Your stop is still your stop. Some traders also close early on a four-hour close against them. Both are defensible. Decide which you will do before the trade, not during it.

Does the daily chart matter? It can. Some traders check it once a week, as a backdrop. Just do not let it become a fourth vote every hour.

I can't watch the London open. Then build your stack around the hours you can watch and keep the same ratios. A one-hour, fifteen-minute and one-minute stack works the same way.

How many pairs? Fewer than you think. Two pairs you know well beat ten you glance at. This series uses EUR/USD and GBP/USD.

What about news? Big scheduled releases can move price straight through any zone on any timeframe. Many traders simply stand aside around them. It is a reasonable rule to write into your plan.

Your turn

EUR/USD, four-hour. The last break was a close below a swing low, and the lower high above it is still standing: bearish. On the one-hour there are two zones. Zone A sits above the 50% line, in premium; zone B sits below it, in discount. You want A — a bearish bias looks for shorts in premium, and B is the wrong half for a short.

Price reaches zone A. Now the five-minute.

Six top-down mistakes

  1. Starting on the five-minute and looking upward for permission. The order is the method. Top-down, not bottom-up.
  2. Too many timeframes. Seven charts will always disagree about something. Three is plenty.
  3. Timeframe shopping. Switching between the 15M, 30M and 2H until one of them shows the trade you already wanted.
  4. Entering straight off a four-hour zone. The stop is enormous, and the size has to shrink to match. The room in a top-down trade comes from taking the stop from the small chart.
  5. Ignoring premium and discount. Buying near the top of the range because the trend is up.
  6. Forgetting that the bias can end. Re-check it at every four-hour close.

The top-down checklist

PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Direction (4H): what was the last break by close, and what close ends it?
  • Location (1H): is price in the right half of the dealing range, at a zone that passes Break, Force, Gap, Fresh?
  • Draw: where is the next obvious pool of liquidity in the direction of the bias?
  • Timing (5M): has there been a sweep and a shift at that zone, inside the written session windows?
  • Risk: is the target at least 2R away, with the stop 2 pips beyond the 5M sweep extreme?

Higher timeframe decides. Lower timeframe executes.

To practise, take one pair on a demo account. Each morning, write down the four-hour bias and the one-hour zone before you look at anything smaller. Then check later whether the day agreed with you. A month of those notes will teach you more about your pair than any number of setups watched in hindsight.

Going deeper

Decide the bias-flip rule in advance. "Stop only" and "stop, or exit on a 4H close against me" are both coherent. The first keeps every trade's risk exactly at 1R and accepts that some trades will be stopped after the bias has already gone. The second cuts some losers early but also exits some trades that would have recovered. Neither is free. Choose, write it down, and record which trades the rule touched.

Conflicts that are not conflicts. A good test: does the lower timeframe's move carry price towards the higher timeframe's location? If the 1H decline is carrying price into 4H discount, it is the pullback. If the 1H decline has already carried price through the 1H zone on a close, the location has failed — and if a 4H close then breaks the defining swing, the bias has failed too. The labels are the same; the order of the closes tells you which situation you are in.

One idea, one trade. If the London window produced a trade on this idea, the New York window is not a second chance at the same idea. Re-run the routine from the top if the 4H has changed; otherwise you are adding size to one opinion.

Record what you skipped. The NO LONG chart above is a skipped trade that would have lost. Some skipped trades would have won. Log both. Without the skips you cannot tell whether your filters remove more bad trades than good ones.

THE RULES
  • Do the routine before London: 4H bias and its ending close, 1H zone and draw, set the alert, close the charts.
  • Only the alert opens the 5M chart.
  • When charts disagree, the higher timeframe wins; resolve it by waiting, never by taking the lower timeframe's side.
  • No longs in premium and no shorts in discount, however good the 5M looks.
  • No 5M shift counts unless it happens at a 1H zone.
  • Management is entry, stop, target. Any exception is written before the trade.

Summary

  • The whole process is one price seen at three magnifications: 4H direction, 1H zone, 5M trigger.
  • The routine — bias, zone, draw, alert, walk away — keeps you off the five-minute until it matters.
  • A lower timeframe moving against a higher one is usually the pullback; wait for it at your zone.
  • A fully aligned trade can still lose. The stop usually tells you before the 4H confirms the change.
  • At 2R, one win pays for two losses: break-even about one in three, before costs.

No trade — wrong half of the range and no location

The 5M stop was hit

lessons.title: SMC Strategy Explained: The 7-Step Execution Stack
lessons.summary: Turn every SMC label you know into one repeatable decision by running seven steps in order — bias, draw, sweep, shift, displacement, return, execute — and stopping at the first no.
lessons.html:
Put every label from this series on one chart. A break of structure. A change of character. Buy-side liquidity above some equal highs. A fair value gap. An order block. Premium and discount. Every one of them can be drawn correctly, and you can still have no idea whether to buy, sell or do nothing.

That is where most people get stuck with Smart Money Concepts. Not the pieces. The order. Ten correct labels with no sequence is just a busy chart, and a busy chart lets you find a reason for whatever you already wanted to do.

This lesson gives the pieces an order. Seven questions, asked one at a time, on three timeframes. We call it the Execution Stack. Nothing in it is new — every step is a rule you have already met in the earlier episodes. What is new is that you answer them in sequence, and you stop the moment one of them says no.

As always in this course: price first, framework second. Each step starts with what the chart observably shows, and only then uses the SMC name for it.

The Execution Stack

The seven steps, each with its one question:

  1. Bias. Which way is the four-hour pointing?
  2. Draw. Where is price likely to be heading — which obvious pool of liquidity sits in that direction?
  3. Sweep. Was liquidity taken against that direction, at our zone, in our hours?
  4. Shift. Did the five-minute structure turn, by a close?
  5. Displacement. Did it turn with force?
  6. Return. Did price come back to where the move started, and react?
  7. Execute. Entry, stop, target, size — and is the target at least 2R away?

Two rules hold the whole thing together. You go in order. And you stop at the first no. No skipping ahead because the chart looks exciting, and no going back to argue with a step that has already failed.

The steps map onto the series. Bias and shift come from market structure (Episodes 1–2). Draw and sweep come from liquidity (Episodes 3–4). Displacement and the gap come from fair value gaps (Episodes 5–6). The return comes from order blocks (Episodes 7–8). The timeframes that hold it together — 4H for direction, 1H for location, 5M for timing — come from top-down analysis (Episodes 9–10).

KEY POINT

Nothing new. Just the order. The Execution Stack is the series' existing rules, stacked in a sequence you can repeat.

Why this order

Each step only means something once the one above it has passed.

A sweep means something when you know which way you are leaning; without a bias, a wick below a low is just a wick. A shift means something straight after a sweep at a zone; a close above a lower high in the middle of nowhere happens all day. A return means something after a move with real force, because a slow drift does not leave a clean zone to return to. And numbers — entry, stop, target — only mean something once there is a setup to put them on.

Run the stack backwards and you get the most common way people trade SMC: see a fair value gap, buy it, then go looking for reasons. The reasons are always there, because a busy chart has a label for everything. The stack makes you find the reasons first and the entry last.

COMMON MISTAKE

Starting at the trigger. A sweep or a gap catches your eye on the five-minute and you work upwards looking for permission. That is the stack upside down, and it will always give you permission.

Step 1: Bias

Four-hour chart. Mark swings with our convention: a swing high is a candle whose high is above the two candles either side of it, and it is only confirmed two candles after it forms (lows mirror this). Breaks are judged on closes. Then ask: what was the last break by close, and is the external structure making higher highs and higher lows, or lower ones?

Then draw the dealing range — from the defining swing low to the swing high of the leg that set the bias — and its 50% line. With a bullish bias we only want longs in the lower half, discount. With a bearish bias, shorts only from the upper half, premium.

Notice the trap at the top of the leg. The bias was bullish while price was still in premium, and a trader who stops reading after "bullish" buys the high. Step one has two halves — direction and location — and it only passes when both are true. If the four-hour structure is overlapping with breaks both ways, there is no bias, and the stack stops here. Lesson 12 shows that day.

Step 2: Draw

Drop to the one-hour. Where is the next obvious pool of liquidity in the direction of the bias? For a long, that means above price: equal highs, an untaken swing high, a previous day's high.

Observably, it is a cluster of obvious highs above price. In framework language, it is the draw on liquidity, or buy-side liquidity (BSL). The resting orders drawn above such highs in SMC diagrams are illustrative — spot FX has no central order book — and the draw is a target to plan around, not a place price owes you a visit.

If there is no obvious pool in the right direction, or it sits right on top of price, step two fails. No room to go means no trade.

While you are on the one-hour, mark the zone you care about: an order block or fair value gap inside discount that passes the checks from Episodes 5–8 (break, force, gap, fresh). That is your point of interest. Set an alert on its top edge and stop watching the chart.

Step 3: Sweep

Price reaches the one-hour zone. Now drop to the five-minute. We want price to take liquidity against the bias first, at our zone. For a long, that means trading below a five-minute swing low and closing back above it.

Location and time are part of the step. A sweep somewhere else does not count: if price takes a low in the middle of nowhere, above the zone, or outside the London (07:00–11:00) and New York (12:00–16:00) windows, step three has not passed.

And remember Episode 3: a sweep on its own is not a reversal. It tells you where something happened. Whether it mattered is the next step's job.

Step 4: Shift

On the way down into the zone, the five-minute has been making lower highs. We need a close above the last one. In our convention that is a change of character (CHOCH): the first close through the last swing against the trend.

Observably: the low was taken, then the last lower high was closed above. The framework calls it a shift. The chart calls it two facts in a row. If it also comes with displacement — step five — Episode 1's definition makes it a market structure shift (MSS): a CHOCH straight after a sweep, with displacement.

Step 5: Displacement

Did the shift happen with force, or did price just drift over the line? Two checks:

  • a candle body at least twice the average body of the previous ten; and
  • a fair value gap left behind in the move.

A shift without displacement is the weakest kind. Price crossed a line; it did not leave in a hurry. We pass.

Step 6: Return

The displacement leg leaves two things behind it: a small order block (the last down candle before the leg — here, the sweep candle) and the fair value gap above it. Together they make one band. We wait for price to come back into it.

It must be the first return — fresh — and we need a reaction: a candle that trades into the band and closes back above it. If price had closed through the bottom of the band instead, the setup would be over. No redrawing it lower. No second chance in the same spot.

COMMON MISTAKE

Entering on the shift candle itself. It feels decisive, but you are buying the top of a fast move with the stop a long way below. Step six exists so that the entry is near the zone and the stop is close.

Step 7: Execute

Four numbers, decided before you click:

  • Entry at the reaction close.
  • Stop two pips beyond the sweep low. If price goes back under the low it just swept, the idea is wrong.
  • Target at the draw — here, the one-hour equal highs.
  • Size from the stop: 1% of the account divided by the stop distance.

Then the check: is the target at least 2R away? If not, the trade does not exist, however good the rest looked.

With the example numbers: entry 1.0777, stop 1.0744 (two pips under the 1.0746 sweep low), so the risk is 33 pips. Target 1.0860, 83 pips away: about 2.5R, which passes. On a £10,000 demo account, 1% is £100; £100 ÷ 33 pips ≈ £3.03 per pip. Your platform's pip value turns that into a lot size. A smaller stop would mean a bigger size and the same £100 at risk — the stop sets the size, never the other way round.

The outcome

And then the boring part. No moving the stop. No closing early because it wobbles. Entry, stop, target. In the example, price dips twice on the way up — each dip is the kind that tempts people to close at break-even — and reaches the equal highs later that session.

That is one trade, start to finish, in order. It is also the least instructive trade in the strategy, because it worked. Lesson 12 shows the ones that matter more: a full loss where every step passed, setups that pass six steps out of seven, and days when the stack stops at step one.

Practice drill: trade or no trade?

Going deeper

Why the steps are binary. Each step is a yes or no that a stranger could check from the chart. That is deliberate. A graded score ("five strong steps and one weak one") invites you to trade the weak one when you are bored. Binary steps make your journal readable: every setup either stopped at a numbered step or was traded, and nothing else.

The timeframes are fixed, not preferences. 4H bias, 1H location and draw, 5M trigger. A 15-minute trigger chart is a legitimate choice, but it is a different strategy with different swing points, sweeps and gaps, and its results go in a separate journal. Mixing them because "the 15-minute looked cleaner today" is choosing the chart that agrees with you.

Where the stack is most fragile. Step five and step six interact. The stronger the displacement, the further price often travels before returning — and sometimes it never returns. That is a cost of the method, not a flaw to fix by entering earlier. Entering on the shift candle changes the stop distance, the R multiple and the failure profile all at once.

What 2R really costs. A minimum of 2R excludes setups where the draw is close, which are often the cleanest-looking ones. The arithmetic behind the rule — and why it matters more than any single step — is in Lesson 12.

Observable versus framework, one last time. Every step can be written in plain chart language: a close beyond a swing, a wick through a low and a close back above it, a body twice the recent average, a three-candle gap, a first return and a close out of it. If you cannot write a step that way for the setup in front of you, the step has not passed — however good the framework story sounds.

THE RULES
  • Run the seven steps in order: bias, draw, sweep, shift, displacement, return, execute.
  • Stop at the first no. A failed step is a skipped setup, not a step to revisit.
  • Bias needs direction and location: longs only from 4H discount, shorts only from 4H premium.
  • The sweep counts only at the 1H zone and inside 07:00–11:00 or 12:00–16:00 London time.
  • Shift is a 5M close through the last swing; displacement needs a body at least 2x the last-10 average and a fair value gap.
  • Enter on the reaction close after the first return; stop 2 pips beyond the sweep; target the draw; at least 2R; risk 1%.

Summary

  • Correct labels do not make a decision. The order does.
  • The Execution Stack: bias, draw, sweep, shift, displacement, return, execute — in order, stop at the first no.
  • Each step only means something once the one above it has passed; running it backwards is how people talk themselves into trades.
  • Execute means four numbers before the click: entry at the reaction close, stop two pips beyond the sweep, target at the draw, size from 1% risk — and at least 2R.
  • Price first. Framework second: every step must be checkable on the chart before you call it anything.

lessons.title: SMC Strategy: The Rules Around the Stack
lessons.summary: Wrap the Execution Stack in the rules that make it a strategy — windows, news, risk, a daily stop — then run it on shorts, losses, near-misses and no-trade days, and leave with the complete playbook, passport and checklist.
lessons.html:
Lesson 11 gave you the seven-step Execution Stack: bias, draw, sweep, shift, displacement, return, execute. In order. Stop at the first no. It ended on a winning trade, which is the least useful thing a strategy can show you.

A strategy is more than its setup. This lesson is everything around the stack: the rules that decide when you may use it, the same stack upside down for shorts, a full loss where every step passed, the trades that pass six steps out of seven, and the days it stops at step one. It is also the course capstone, so it finishes with the complete playbook, three worked trades, the strategy passport and the full pre-trade checklist.

Price first. Framework second. Nothing here asks you to know what anyone else intends. Every rule is something you can check on a clock, a calendar or a chart.

The rules around the stack

Time. Triggers are only taken in the London and New York mornings: 07:00–11:00 and 12:00–16:00, London time. Outside those windows, step three cannot pass, however clean the sweep looks. The windows are our written choice; what matters is that you fix them and stop negotiating with them.

News. No new trades in the 30 minutes either side of a major scheduled release for either currency in the pair. Check the calendar before the session, not after the candle.

Risk. 1% of the account per trade, sized from the stop. A trade needs at least 2R to the draw, or it does not exist. Two losses in a day and you are done for the day. Not angry, not chasing. Done.

Rule changes. The rules do not change during the week. If you want to change one, write the change down and make it on Sunday, before the next week's first session.

KEY POINT

The rules around the stack are not filters you apply when you feel like it. They are part of the steps: outside the window, step three fails; under 2R, step seven fails.

Shorts: the stack upside down

Every step mirrors. Bias bearish on the four-hour, price up in premium. The draw is below: sell-side liquidity (SSL) under obvious lows. The sweep is a trade above a five-minute high that closes back below it. The shift is a close below the last higher low, with displacement. The return is back up into the order block and gap the drop came from, and the reaction is a close back below that band. Stop two pips above the sweep high. Target the lows.

A full loss

Pound-dollar again, a different day, a long. Four-hour bullish, price in discount. Draw above at the previous day's high. A sweep at the one-hour zone inside the London window. A shift. Displacement. A clean return and a reaction close. Seven ticks, and 2.4R on the measure.

Price climbs a little, stalls, and then closes back through the sweep low. Stopped. A full one-R loss.

Every step passed. The loss is still a loss. This is the most important idea in the series: following the rules does not mean you win. It means your losses are the size you planned.

The arithmetic is simple. If every win is at least 2R and every loss is 1R, one win pays for two losses. Before costs, you need to be right roughly one time in three just to break even; spreads and commissions push that higher. We are not telling you how often this stack wins. We cannot, from synthetic examples. That is something you measure yourself, on a demo account, over a lot of trades.

Six out of seven

The hardest trade is the one that almost qualifies.

Missing that winner is part of the method. The point of the stack is to take the same kind of trade every time, so your results actually tell you something. A journal that mixes displaced shifts with drifts cannot tell you whether either works.

The second kind of six out of seven fails at the last step. Everything passes, but the draw is too close: under 2R.

A no-trade day

Plenty of days, the stack stops at step one. The four-hour chart is chopping sideways: breaks in both directions, overlapping swings, no clean sequence of higher highs and higher lows or lower ones. No bias. No trade, on this pair, today.

You will be tempted to drop to the five-minute and find something. There is always something on the five-minute. That is exactly why it does not get a vote. Close the charts, check the other pair, or do not trade at all. Doing nothing is a position too.

Quick answers

Can I use a 15-minute trigger chart instead of the 5M? Yes, if you keep it fixed. A different trigger chart is a different strategy; test and journal it as one.

What if price never comes back for step six? Then there is no trade. Some of the best-looking moves leave without you. That is the price of waiting for a reaction.

Can I put a limit order in the zone instead? Plenty of traders do. It gets you in more often — and into more of the zones that fail. We wait for the reaction close. Pick one and stick to it.

How many trades a week? There is no target number. Some weeks the stack passes a few times; some weeks not once. The stack decides, not the calendar.

The journal

The last piece is not on the chart. For every setup, record: date, pair, session, the step where it stopped, and — if you traded — entry, stop, target and the result in R. Save a screenshot. Log the setups that stopped at step one too.

Once a week, read it back. Where do your losses cluster? Which step do you keep wanting to skip? That is where your next improvement is hiding. Rule changes that come out of the review are written down and made on Sunday.

Your turn

Euro-dollar. The four-hour is bullish. Price has pulled back into discount and reached a one-hour zone. On the five-minute it trades below a low and closes back above it. Which step are you on? Step three has passed; you are waiting for step four, a close above the last lower high. No trade yet.

The shift comes, with a big body and a gap. Price returns to the zone it left and closes back above it. Enter? Not yet: step seven first. Stop under the sweep low, target at the draw, measure it. It comes to about 1.5R. Six out of seven is a no.

Seven strategy mistakes

  1. Starting at step three. A sweep with no bias is just a wick.
  2. Entering on the shift candle. Step six exists for a reason.
  3. Taking a target under 2R because the rest looked so good.
  4. Trading outside your windows because you happened to be awake.
  5. Moving the stop when price gets close to it.
  6. The third trade after two losses. Done means done.
  7. Changing the rules every week. Then you never find out whether the old ones worked.

The complete playbook

Before the session (per pair). (1) 4H: mark swings (two candles each side, confirmed two candles later), note the last break by close, write the bias — bullish, bearish or none. None ends the day for that pair. (2) Draw the dealing range and its 50% line; note whether price is in discount or premium. (3) 1H: mark the draw — the obvious pool in the bias direction — and the fresh order block or gap inside the correct half. Set an alert on it. (4) Check the calendar and block 30 minutes either side of major releases.

In the window. (5) Price reaches the 1H zone. (6) 5M sweep at the zone: a trade through a swing low (longs) and a close back above it. (7) Shift: a close through the last lower high. (8) Displacement: a body at least twice the last-ten average and a fair value gap. (9) Return: the first move back into the OB + FVG band and a reaction close out of it. A close through the band ends the setup.

Execute. (10) Entry at the reaction close; stop two pips beyond the sweep; target the draw; at least 2R. (11) Size: 1% of the account ÷ stop distance. (12) Hands off: no moving the stop, no early close. (13) Journal it, whatever happened.

Each was planned to the pip before entry, and each journal line reads the same way: seven ticks, no rule breaks.

The strategy passport

  • Market: major FX pairs (examples use EUR/USD and GBP/USD). 4H for bias, 1H for location and the draw, 5M for the trigger.
  • Wait for: a 4H bias from the last close-based break, price in discount for longs (premium for shorts), an obvious pool in the bias direction as the draw, and a fresh 1H order block or gap in that half.
  • Trigger: inside 07:00–11:00 or 12:00–16:00 London time, a 5M sweep at the 1H zone, a CHOCH by close with displacement, the first return into the 5M OB + FVG and a reaction close — entry at that close.
  • Stop: two pips beyond the sweep extreme. Risk 1%, size from the stop, never moved.
  • Target: the draw on liquidity, at least 2R away, or no trade.
  • Avoid: no 4H bias; sweeps away from the zone or outside the windows; shifts without displacement; entering on the shift candle; 30 minutes either side of major news; a third trade after two losses; mid-week rule changes.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • 4H bias written down from the last break by close (bullish, bearish or none — none means no trade)
  • Price in 4H discount for a long, premium for a short (below or above the 50% line)
  • 1H draw marked: an obvious liquidity pool in the bias direction, with room to reach it
  • 1H zone marked: a fresh order block or fair value gap in the correct half of the range
  • Calendar checked: no major release within 30 minutes either side
  • Inside 07:00–11:00 or 12:00–16:00 London time
  • Fewer than two losses already today
  • 5M sweep at the 1H zone: through a swing and a close back inside
  • 5M shift: a close through the last lower high (long) or higher low (short)
  • Displacement: a body at least 2x the last-ten average and a fair value gap
  • First return into the OB + FVG band, then a reaction close out of it (no close through the band)
  • Entry at the reaction close, stop 2 pips beyond the sweep, target at the draw, measured at 2R or more
  • Size = 1% of the account ÷ stop distance
  • Journal line and screenshot saved, including the step where any skipped setup stopped

Going deeper

The loss belongs in the plan. A run of losses is ordinary in any method that needs only a minority of winners to break even. Two losses and done caps a bad day at roughly 2% before costs; it does not stop a bad week. Read the journal: losses with no rule breaks spread across many steps are the method's normal cost; losses that cluster after one particular step are a pattern worth testing.

Skips are data too. Log what skipped setups would have done. If six-of-seven drifts keep reaching the draw, you have a hypothesis — test it as a separate strategy with its own journal, never by quietly relaxing step five mid-week.

Correlation. EUR/USD and GBP/USD often move together against the dollar. Two longs on the same morning can be one idea twice. Decide in advance whether that counts as one trade's risk or two, and write it in your rules.

Costs scale with tight stops. A spread of one to two pips is small against a 33-pip stop and large against an 8-pip one. Measure your own costs on demo; they move the break-even point.

THE RULES
  • Triggers only 07:00–11:00 and 12:00–16:00 London time; outside them step three fails.
  • No new trades within 30 minutes either side of a major scheduled release.
  • Risk 1% per trade, sized from the stop. At least 2R to the draw, or no trade.
  • Two losses in a day: done for the day.
  • The stop and target are never moved after entry.
  • Rules change only on Sunday, in writing.

Summary

  • The rules around the stack — windows, news, 1% risk, at least 2R, two losses and done, Sunday-only rule changes — are part of the steps, not optional filters.
  • Shorts are the same stack upside down: premium, SSL as the draw, a sweep above a high, a close below the last higher low.
  • A trade can pass all seven steps and lose. The rules make your losses the size you planned; at 2R, one win pays for two losses before costs.
  • Six out of seven is a no, even when the skipped trade would have worked. No bias means no trade, and the 5M does not get a vote.
  • Journal the step where every setup stopped. Price first. Framework second.
